segments.title: Unverified Ancestry and Priestly Exclusion
segments.gist: Describes families unable to prove their Israelite descent and priests excluded from the priesthood pending Urim and Thummim.

segments.title: Total Congregation and Servants
segments.gist: States the total number of returnees and their servants, singers, and animals.

segments.title: Freewill Offerings and Settlement
segments.gist: Recounts the freewill offerings given for the temple and the settlement of the people in their towns.

3.summary: Under Zerubbabel and Jeshua, the returned exiles rebuild the altar and resume burnt offerings and the Feast of Tabernacles. They lay the foundation of the temple with music and praise, but the celebration is mixed with weeping from older men who remember the former house.

segments.title: Altar rebuilt and offerings resume
segments.gist: The people gather in Jerusalem, rebuild the altar, offer burnt offerings, and keep the Feast of Tabernacles despite fear of surrounding peoples.

segments.title: Work on temple foundation begins
segments.gist: In the second year, Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the returned exiles appoint Levites to oversee the work on the house of God.

segments.title: Foundation laid with praise
segments.gist: When builders lay the foundation, priests and Levites with trumpets and cymbals praise the LORD, singing that his mercy endures forever.

segments.title: Mixed weeping and shouting
segments.gist: Old men who saw the former temple weep aloud, while many others shout for joy, so the sounds of weeping and joy cannot be distinguished.

4.summary: Opposition arises against the rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem. The adversaries first offer to help, are refused, and then work to frustrate the building throughout the reigns of Cyrus and Darius, eventually sending a letter to King Artaxerxes that halts the work.

segments.title: Adversaries Request to Help Build
segments.gist: Enemies of Judah and Benjamin ask Zerubbabel and the fathers to let them help build the temple, claiming to seek God.

segments.title: Request Refused; Opposition Begins
segments.gist: Zerubbabel and the leaders refuse the offer, and the people of the land weaken the Jews' hands and hire counselors to frustrate the work.

segments.title: Letter to King Artaxerxes
segments.gist: The adversaries send a letter to Artaxerxes accusing the Jews of rebuilding a rebellious city and warning that it will harm the king's revenue.

segments.title: King's Reply Orders Work to Cease
segments.gist: Artaxerxes replies, commanding that the building stop until further order, so the Jews cannot rebuild the rebellious city.

segments.title: Work on Temple Halted
segments.gist: The king's letter is read before Rehum and others, who go to Jerusalem and force the Jews to stop building until the second year of Darius.

5.summary: The prophets Haggai and Zechariah encourage Zerubbabel and Jeshua to resume rebuilding the temple. When the Persian governor Tattenai questions their authority, the Jews appeal to Cyrus's decree, and Tattenai sends a letter to King Darius asking for a search of the royal archives.

segments.title: Prophets urge rebuilding
segments.gist: Haggai and Zechariah prophesy to the Jews, and Zerubbabel and Jeshua begin rebuilding the temple.

segments.title: Tattenai questions the work
segments.gist: Governor Tattenai and his companions ask who authorized the rebuilding and request the names of the workers.

segments.title: Tattenai's letter to Darius
segments.gist: Tattenai sends a letter to King Darius reporting the Jews' claim of a decree from Cyrus and asking for verification.

segments.title: Jews recount Cyrus's decree
segments.gist: The Jews explain that Cyrus commanded the temple's rebuilding and returned the gold and silver vessels taken by Nebuchadnezzar.

6.summary: King Darius orders a search of the archives, finds Cyrus's decree authorizing the rebuilding of the Jerusalem temple, and commands that the work be funded and protected. The Jews complete the temple, celebrate its dedication, and keep the Passover and Feast of Unleavened Bread.

segments.title: Darius orders search of archives
segments.gist: King Darius commands a search of the Babylonian archives, and a scroll is found in Achmetha recording Cyrus's decree to rebuild the temple.

segments.title: Darius commands funding and protection
segments.gist: Darius decrees that the provincial officials must not hinder the Jews, but must fund the building and provide sacrifices, with severe penalties for disobedience.

segments.title: Temple completed
segments.gist: The elders of the Jews build and prosper under the prophets Haggai and Zechariah, and the temple is finished in the sixth year of Darius.

segments.title: Temple dedication
segments.gist: The children of Israel, priests, Levites, and others joyfully dedicate the house of God with offerings and set the priests and Levites in their divisions.

segments.title: Passover and Unleavened Bread
segments.gist: The returned exiles keep the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days with joy, because the Lord had turned the heart of the king of Assyria toward them.

7.summary: Ezra 7 introduces Ezra, a scribe skilled in the law of Moses, who comes up from Babylon to Jerusalem with a group of exiles. King Artaxerxes grants him a letter of authorization, providing resources for the temple and empowering him to appoint magistrates and teach the law. Ezra then gathers leaders and prepares for the journey, acknowledging God's hand upon him.

segments.title: Ezra's lineage and purpose
segments.gist: Ezra's genealogy from Aaron is listed, and his commitment to study and teach the law is described.

segments.title: Artaxerxes' letter to Ezra
segments.gist: King Artaxerxes authorizes Ezra to return with exiles, provides temple funding, and grants judicial authority.

segments.title: Ezra's blessing and gathering
segments.gist: Ezra blesses God for the king's favor and gathers leading men of Israel to go with him.

8.summary: Ezra recounts the heads of families who returned with him from Babylon to Jerusalem, including priests and Levites. He proclaims a fast at the river Ahava to seek God's protection, then assigns priests to guard the offerings for the temple. The chapter ends with the travelers arriving safely in Jerusalem and delivering the treasures.

segments.title: Genealogy of Returning Exiles
segments.gist: A list of the family heads and their descendants who accompanied Ezra from Babylon to Jerusalem.

segments.title: Levites and Temple Servants Recruited
segments.gist: Ezra finds no Levites among the people and sends for temple servants to join the returning group.

segments.title: Fast Proclaimed at Ahava
segments.gist: Ezra calls for a fast to humble themselves and seek God's protection for the journey.

segments.title: Priests Appointed to Guard Offerings
segments.gist: Ezra assigns twelve priests to guard the silver, gold, and vessels for the temple.

segments.title: Safe Arrival and Delivery of Treasures
segments.gist: The group travels safely to Jerusalem, delivers the offerings, and presents them in the temple.

9.summary: After the temple was rebuilt, officials report to Ezra that the people of Israel, including priests and Levites, have intermarried with the surrounding peoples and adopted their abominations. Ezra tears his garment, plucks out his hair, and sits astonished until the evening sacrifice, then falls on his knees in a prayer of confession, recounting God's past grace and the nation's repeated unfaithfulness.

segments.title: Officials report intermarriage
segments.gist: Princes tell Ezra that the people, priests, and Levites have not separated from the surrounding nations but have taken their daughters as wives, mixing the holy seed.

segments.title: Ezra's prayer of confession
segments.gist: Ezra kneels and prays, confessing the people's sins, acknowledging God's past mercy, and pleading for mercy despite their renewed unfaithfulness.

10.summary: While Ezra prays and confesses Israel's sin of intermarriage with foreign peoples, the people gather in tears and agree to put away their foreign wives. A proclamation is issued for all to assemble in Jerusalem, and the assembly agrees to the covenant. Because of the rainy weather and the large number of cases, a commission of heads is appointed to handle the matter, and the chapter closes with a list of those who had taken foreign wives.

segments.title: Ezra's Prayer and the People's Response
segments.gist: Ezra prays and confesses, and Shechaniah proposes a covenant to put away foreign wives.

segments.title: Assembly Summoned to Jerusalem
segments.gist: Ezra makes the leaders swear an oath, and a proclamation summons all exiles to Jerusalem under penalty.

segments.title: Ezra Addresses the Assembled People
segments.gist: The people gather trembling in the rain, and Ezra commands them to separate from foreign wives.

segments.title: People Agree and Propose a Plan
segments.gist: The assembly agrees, and proposes that leaders handle the cases by set times due to the heavy rain.

segments.title: Commission Investigates the Cases
segments.gist: Opponents are named, and the appointed heads investigate and finish the matter by the first month.

segments.title: List of Men with Foreign Wives
segments.gist: A list of priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, and other Israelites who had taken foreign wives.

1.summary: Nehemiah, a cupbearer to King Artaxerxes in Shushan, receives news from his brother Hanani that Jerusalem's walls are broken down and its gates burned. He mourns, fasts, and prays, confessing Israel's sins and reminding God of His promise to gather His people, then asks for favor with the king.

segments.title: Nehemiah hears of Jerusalem's ruin
segments.gist: Hanani and other men from Judah tell Nehemiah that Jerusalem's wall is broken and its gates burned, leaving him devastated.

segments.title: Nehemiah's prayer of confession
segments.gist: Nehemiah mourns, fasts, and prays, confessing Israel's sins and asking God to remember His promise and grant him favor with the king.

2.summary: Nehemiah, cupbearer to King Artaxerxes, is sad before the king and asks permission to return to Jerusalem to rebuild its walls. The king grants his request and provides letters and supplies. Nehemiah travels to Jerusalem, inspects the broken walls by night, and urges the leaders to rebuild, despite opposition from Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem.

segments.title: Nehemiah's Request to the King
segments.gist: Nehemiah, sad before King Artaxerxes, explains his desire to rebuild Jerusalem and asks for letters and supplies, which the king grants.

segments.title: Arrival and Opposition
segments.gist: Nehemiah arrives in Jerusalem and is met with displeasure from Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite.

segments.title: Night Inspection of the Walls
segments.gist: Nehemiah secretly inspects the broken walls and gates at night, then urges the officials to rebuild, attributing his success to God's hand.

segments.title: Call to Rebuild
segments.gist: Nehemiah tells the leaders about the ruined state of Jerusalem and his commission from the king, and they agree to rebuild.

segments.title: Mockery and Response
segments.gist: Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem mock the Jews, but Nehemiah replies that God will prosper them and they have no share in Jerusalem.

3.summary: Nehemiah records how the wall of Jerusalem was rebuilt by many groups working on assigned sections. Priests, rulers, craftsmen, and families each repaired a portion near their homes, while nobles from Tekoa shirked the work. The chapter lists the builders and their sections, showing the cooperative effort that restored the wall.

segments.title: Eliashib and priests rebuild gates
segments.gist: Eliashib the high priest and fellow priests rebuild the Sheep Gate and its doors, and other groups repair nearby sections.

segments.title: Repairs by various groups
segments.gist: Groups including men of Gibeon, Mizpah, and rulers repair gates, walls, and towers, with some working opposite their homes.

segments.title: Valley Gate and Dung Gate
segments.gist: Hanun and the inhabitants of Zanoah repair the Valley Gate and the Dung Gate, including their doors and a thousand cubits of wall.

segments.title: Pool of Siloam to house of Eliashib
segments.gist: Shallun repairs the Fountain Gate, and other leaders repair sections from the pool of Siloam up to the house of Eliashib.

segments.title: Priests and Tekoites repair
segments.gist: Priests from the plain, Benjamin and Hasshub, and the Tekoites repair sections, though their nobles refuse to work.

segments.title: Horse Gate to Sheep Gate
segments.gist: Priests, merchants, and goldsmiths repair the wall from the Horse Gate up to the Sheep Gate, each opposite their own house.

4.summary: When Sanballat and Tobiah mock the Jews' rebuilding of Jerusalem's wall and threaten attack, Nehemiah stations guards and arms the workers. The builders continue with tools in one hand and weapons in the other, trusting God for protection.

segments.title: Enemies Mock the Building
segments.gist: Sanballat ridicules the Jews and Tobiah adds a scornful remark about their wall, provoking Nehemiah's prayer.

segments.title: Nehemiah Prays Against Enemies
segments.gist: Nehemiah asks God to turn the enemies' reproach back on them and not cover their sin.

segments.title: Threat and Guard Posted
segments.gist: When the enemies plot an attack, the Jews pray and set a watch day and night.

segments.title: Workers Discouraged by Threats
segments.gist: Judah laments the workers' strength is failing, and nearby enemies repeatedly warn of imminent attack.

segments.title: Defense Organized and Enemy Deterred
segments.gist: Nehemiah arms families by families and encourages them to fight for their homes; the enemies withdraw when they hear of the preparations.

segments.title: Builders Work Armed
segments.gist: From then on, half the men guard while the other half build with weapons ready, and Nehemiah and his men stay dressed for action.

5.summary: Nehemiah confronts the internal crisis of debt slavery among the Jews, rebukes the nobles and rulers for oppressing their own people, and secures their oath to restore lands and cancel debts. He then recounts his own twelve years of generous governance as governor, refusing the usual allowances and providing for many at his table.

segments.title: Outcry of the oppressed
segments.gist: Many Jews cry out against their brethren because of famine, debt, and the mortgaging of lands and children to survive.

segments.title: Nehemiah rebukes the nobles
segments.gist: Nehemiah is angry, calls an assembly, and charges the nobles with exacting usury from their own brethren, demanding restoration.

segments.title: Nehemiah's generous governorship
segments.gist: Nehemiah recounts twelve years of not taking the governor's allowance and providing daily for many at his own expense.

6.summary: Nehemiah's enemies Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem try repeatedly to stop the rebuilding of Jerusalem's wall—through invitations to meet, false accusations of rebellion, and a hired prophet's scare tactic—but Nehemiah refuses to be distracted or intimidated. The wall is completed in fifty-two days, and the surrounding nations are dismayed, while Tobiah's allies among the nobles continue to correspond with him against Nehemiah.

segments.title: Enemies Plot, Nehemiah Refuses
segments.gist: Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem invite Nehemiah to meet, but he declines, saying he is doing a great work and cannot come down.

segments.title: False Accusation of Rebellion
segments.gist: Sanballat sends an open letter accusing Nehemiah of planning rebellion, but Nehemiah denies it and prays for strength.

segments.title: Hired Prophet's Scare Tactic
segments.gist: Shemaiah tries to lure Nehemiah into the temple for safety, but Nehemiah refuses, recognizing the plot to make him sin and lose credibility.

segments.title: Wall Completed in Fifty-Two Days
segments.gist: The wall is finished in fifty-two days, and the enemies are cast down, recognizing the work was done by God.

segments.title: Tobiah's Noble Allies
segments.gist: The nobles of Judah correspond with Tobiah and report Nehemiah's words to him, while Tobiah sends letters to intimidate Nehemiah.

7.summary: After the wall is finished and the gates set, Nehemiah appoints gatekeepers and gives charge to Hanani and Hananiah, then finds a register of the first exiles who returned from Babylon and records their numbers, along with the gifts given for the work.

segments.title: Nehemiah Appoints Guards
segments.gist: Nehemiah sets gatekeepers and charges Hanani and Hananiah to guard Jerusalem and keep the gates shut until the sun is hot.

segments.title: Register of Returning Exiles
segments.gist: Nehemiah finds a register of the first exiles who returned from Babylon and records the number of the people of Israel.

segments.title: List of Families and Towns
segments.gist: The register lists the families of the people, priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, and temple servants who returned.

segments.title: Priests, Levites, and Servants
segments.gist: The list continues with the numbers of priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, and temple servants, including the children of Solomon's servants.

segments.title: Unverified Ancestry and Totals
segments.gist: Some families could not prove their Israelite ancestry, and the total number of the congregation is given.

segments.title: Gifts and Settlement
segments.gist: The chapter ends with the gifts given by the governor and others for the work, and the people settle in their cities.

8.summary: All the people gather at the Water Gate and ask Ezra the scribe to read the book of the law. Ezra reads from morning until midday while the Levites explain the meaning, and the people weep. Nehemiah and Ezra tell them to stop mourning and celebrate, because the day is holy, and the people go home to eat and share with those who have nothing. On the second day the heads of families discover the command to dwell in booths during the seventh month, so they build booths and keep the feast with great joy, as had not been done since Joshua's time.

segments.title: People gather for the law
segments.gist: All the people assemble at the Water Gate and ask Ezra to bring and read the book of the law of Moses.

segments.title: Ezra reads and Levites explain
segments.gist: Ezra reads from morning until midday, the people stand, and the Levites help them understand the reading.

segments.title: Nehemiah and Ezra calm the people
segments.gist: Nehemiah, Ezra, and the Levites tell the weeping people that the day is holy, to eat, drink, and share with the poor, for the joy of the Lord is their strength.

segments.title: Feast of booths restored
segments.gist: On the second day the family heads find the command to dwell in booths, so the people build booths and keep the feast with great joy, as not done since Joshua's days.

9.summary: The people of Israel gather in sackcloth and fasting to confess their sins, and the Levites lead a long prayer recounting God's creation, covenant with Abraham, deliverance from Egypt, provision in the wilderness, and repeated mercy despite Israel's rebellion. The prayer concludes with a confession of present oppression under foreign kings and a covenant to obey.

segments.title: People gather and confess
segments.gist: Israelites assemble with fasting, sackcloth, and dust, separating themselves and confessing their sins and the iniquities of their fathers.

segments.title: Praise and Abrahamic covenant
segments.gist: The Levites bless God as creator and recount his choice of Abram, the covenant, and the promise of the land.

segments.title: Exodus and wilderness provision
segments.gist: The prayer recalls God's signs against Pharaoh, the parting of the sea, guidance by cloud and fire, and provision of manna and water.

segments.title: Rebellion and God's mercy
segments.gist: Despite Israel's pride and rebellion, God in his great mercy did not forsake them in the wilderness but continued to lead and provide.

segments.title: Conquest, kings, and repeated mercy
segments.gist: God gave them kingdoms and land, but the people repeatedly rebelled; God delivered them to enemies yet in mercy heard their cry and saved them many times.

segments.title: Confession of present oppression
segments.gist: The prayer acknowledges God's justice and confesses that despite his faithfulness, the people are now servants under foreign kings, and they make a written covenant.

10.summary: The chapter records the sealed covenant in which Nehemiah, the priests, Levites, and leading men bind themselves by oath to keep God's law. The people pledge specific obligations: not to intermarry with surrounding peoples, to observe the Sabbath and sabbatical year, and to support the temple service with firstfruits and tithes.

segments.title: List of those who sealed
segments.gist: Names of the governor, priests, Levites, and chief men who put their seal to the covenant.

segments.title: People bind themselves by oath
segments.gist: The rest of the people join in a curse and oath to walk in God's law and avoid intermarriage and Sabbath trade.

segments.title: Temple service and tithe pledges
segments.gist: Specific commitments are made for the temple tax, firstfruits, wood offering, and tithes to support priests and Levites.

11.summary: The leaders and a tenth of the people are chosen by lot to live in Jerusalem, while the rest remain in other towns. The chapter lists the families and individuals who resettled in Jerusalem and records the villages in Judah and Benjamin where the remaining people lived.

segments.title: People chosen to dwell in Jerusalem
segments.gist: The rulers live in Jerusalem, and the rest cast lots to bring one in ten to live there, while the others stay in their towns.

segments.title: Families of Judah and Benjamin in Jerusalem
segments.gist: The chapter lists the leaders and families from Judah and Benjamin who settled in Jerusalem, including their numbers.

segments.title: Priests and Levites in Jerusalem
segments.gist: It names the priests and Levites who lived in Jerusalem, along with their ancestral houses and duties.

segments.title: Levites and temple servants in Jerusalem
segments.gist: The Levites, gatekeepers, and temple servants (Nethinims) who resided in Jerusalem are listed with their roles.

segments.title: Temple servants and singers outside Jerusalem
segments.gist: The Nethinims lived in Ophel, and the singers and Levites were appointed by the king's command in their villages.

segments.title: Villages of Judah and Benjamin
segments.gist: The chapter records the towns and villages in Judah and Benjamin where the remaining Israelites lived, including their genealogies.

12.summary: Nehemiah 12 records the priests and Levites who returned with Zerubbabel, the high priests down to Jaddua, and the dedication of Jerusalem's wall with two thanksgiving processions, music, and sacrifices. It closes with arrangements for temple contributions and the purification of the people, gates, and wall.

segments.title: Priests and Levites Registered
segments.gist: Lists the priests and Levites who came up with Zerubbabel and Jeshua, and the high priests down to Jaddua.

segments.title: Dedication of the Wall
segments.gist: Nehemiah assembles the Levites and leads two thanksgiving companies along the wall with music and sacrifices.

segments.title: Temple Contributions Appointed
segments.gist: Men are appointed over storerooms for offerings, and the people bring portions for priests and Levites.

13.summary: Nehemiah returns to Jerusalem after reporting to the Persian king and finds several reforms broken: Tobiah has been given a room in the temple, the Levites' portions have been withheld, the Sabbath is being violated by traders, and men have married foreign women. Nehemiah confronts each abuse, restores the tithes and temple service, enforces Sabbath closure of the gates, and deals harshly with mixed marriages, ending with a plea for God to remember him.

segments.title: Nehemiah returns and reads the law
segments.gist: While the book of Moses is read aloud, the people separate themselves from foreigners, and Nehemiah learns that Tobiah has been given a room in the temple.

segments.title: Nehemiah expels Tobiah
segments.gist: Nehemiah returns from the king, throws Tobiah's household goods out of the temple chamber, and orders the room cleansed and restored for temple use.

segments.title: Tithes restored for Levites
segments.gist: Nehemiah discovers the Levites have fled to their fields because their portions were not given, rebukes the rulers, and restores the tithe system with trustworthy treasurers.

segments.title: Sabbath trading stopped
segments.gist: Nehemiah sees men treading winepresses and selling goods on the Sabbath, rebukes the nobles, orders the gates shut, and threatens the merchants to keep the Sabbath holy.

segments.title: Mixed marriages confronted
segments.gist: Nehemiah contends with Jews who married women of Ashdod, Ammon, and Moab, curses and beats some, and drives out the son of the high priest, ending with a prayer for remembrance.

1.summary: King Ahasuerus of Persia holds a lavish feast in Shushan for his nobles and officials, displaying his wealth for 180 days and then hosting a seven-day banquet for all the people. On the final day, he commands Queen Vashti to appear before the guests to show off her beauty, but she refuses. Enraged, the king consults his wise men, who advise him to depose Vashti and issue a royal decree that all wives must honor their husbands, so that the queen's defiance not spread to other women.

segments.title: Ahasuerus's royal feast
segments.gist: King Ahasuerus hosts a 180-day feast for his nobles and officials, displaying his wealth and glory.

segments.title: Seven-day banquet in Shushan
segments.gist: The king holds a seven-day feast for all people in Shushan, with lavish decorations and unlimited royal wine.

segments.title: Vashti refuses the king's command
segments.gist: On the seventh day, the king orders Vashti to appear before the guests, but she refuses, angering him greatly.

segments.title: Counsel to depose Vashti
segments.gist: The king's wise men advise him to depose Vashti and decree that all wives must honor their husbands, lest other women follow her example.

segments.title: Decree issued to all provinces
segments.gist: The king approves the counsel, sends letters to every province in its own language, and Vashti is removed as queen.

2.summary: After King Ahasuerus's anger cools, his servants propose gathering beautiful young virgins to replace Queen Vashti. Esther, a Jewish orphan raised by her cousin Mordecai, is taken to the palace and finds favor with the king's chamberlain Hegai. Mordecai advises her to hide her heritage, and when her turn comes, she wins the king's love and is made queen. Later, Mordecai uncovers a plot against the king's life and reports it through Esther, and the conspirators are hanged.

segments.title: Search for a new queen
segments.gist: The king's servants suggest gathering fair young virgins to replace Vashti, and the king agrees.

segments.title: Esther taken to palace
segments.gist: Esther, Mordecai's orphan cousin, is brought to the palace and pleases Hegai, who favors her.

segments.title: Esther hides her identity
segments.gist: Esther keeps her Jewish heritage secret on Mordecai's advice, while he checks on her daily.

segments.title: Preparation of the women
segments.gist: Each woman undergoes twelve months of purification before spending a night with the king.

segments.title: Esther becomes queen
segments.gist: Esther wins favor with all who see her, and the king loves her and crowns her queen.

segments.title: Mordecai uncovers a plot
segments.gist: Mordecai learns of a plot to kill the king, tells Esther, and the conspirators are hanged.

3.summary: King Ahasuerus promotes Haman above all his princes, and everyone at the king's gate bows to him except Mordecai the Jew. Enraged, Haman persuades the king to issue a decree to destroy all Jews throughout the empire, and the decree is sealed and published.

segments.title: Haman exalted, Mordecai refuses to bow
segments.gist: Ahasuerus promotes Haman and commands all servants to bow, but Mordecai refuses, explaining he is a Jew.

segments.title: Haman's anger and plot against Jews
segments.gist: Haman is filled with wrath and, learning Mordecai's identity, plots to destroy all Jews throughout the kingdom.

segments.title: Haman offers king silver for destruction
segments.gist: Haman tells the king about a people who keep separate laws and offers ten thousand talents of silver for their destruction.

segments.title: King grants Haman authority and ring
segments.gist: The king gives Haman his ring and authorizes him to do as he pleases with the people and the silver.

segments.title: Decree written and published
segments.gist: Scribes write the decree in every language, it is sealed with the king's ring, and couriers deliver it to destroy all Jews on the thirteenth day of Adar.

4.summary: Mordecai and the Jews mourn in sackcloth over Haman's decree to destroy them. Esther learns of it, and after initial hesitation she agrees to approach the king uninvited, asking the Jews to fast with her.

segments.title: Mordecai mourns the decree
segments.gist: Mordecai tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth and ashes, and cries bitterly in the city, while the Jews mourn in every province.

segments.title: Esther learns and sends clothes
segments.gist: Esther's maids and eunuchs tell her of Mordecai's mourning; she sends clothes to him, but he refuses, and she sends Hathach to learn why.

segments.title: Mordecai explains the plot
segments.gist: Mordecai tells Hathach of Haman's plot and the money promised, and gives him a copy of the decree to show Esther, urging her to plead with the king.

segments.title: Mordecai's challenge to Esther
segments.gist: Mordecai warns Esther not to think she will escape, and says she may have come to the kingdom for such a time as this.

segments.title: Esther agrees to act
segments.gist: Esther asks Mordecai and all the Jews to fast for three days, resolves to go to the king uninvited, and says, 'If I perish, I perish.'

5.summary: Esther approaches King Ahasuerus uninvited and finds favor when he extends his golden scepter; she invites him and Haman to a banquet, and at that banquet she asks them to return the next day. Haman leaves elated but is infuriated by Mordecai's refusal to bow, and at his wife's suggestion he has a gallows built to hang Mordecai.

segments.title: Esther Approaches the King
segments.gist: Esther stands in the inner court; the king extends his scepter and offers her up to half his kingdom.

segments.title: Esther Invites King and Haman
segments.gist: Esther asks the king and Haman to come to a banquet she has prepared, and the king agrees.

segments.title: Haman's Joy and Rage
segments.gist: Haman rejoices over the invitation but is enraged by Mordecai; his wife suggests building a gallows for him.

6.summary: During a sleepless night, King Ahasuerus has the royal chronicles read and learns that Mordecai once foiled an assassination plot but was never rewarded. When Haman arrives to ask permission to hang Mordecai, the king instead orders Haman to publicly honor Mordecai, leaving Haman humiliated and his family predicting his downfall.

segments.title: King reads chronicles
segments.gist: Ahasuerus, unable to sleep, orders the chronicles read and hears how Mordecai exposed the plot of Bigthan and Teresh.

segments.title: Mordecai's unrewarded deed
segments.gist: The king asks what honor Mordecai received; his servants answer that nothing was done for him.

segments.title: Haman proposes honor
segments.gist: Haman enters to ask for Mordecai's hanging, but the king asks how to honor a deserving man; Haman, thinking himself the man, suggests royal robes, horse, and public proclamation.

segments.title: Haman honors Mordecai
segments.gist: The king orders Haman to do exactly as he proposed for Mordecai, and Haman parades Mordecai through the city street.

segments.title: Haman's family foretells fall
segments.gist: Mordecai returns to the gate while Haman mourns; his wife Zeresh and friends say Mordecai's rise means Haman's certain downfall, and the king's eunuchs hurry him to Esther's banquet.

7.summary: At Esther's second banquet, the king again offers to grant her request, and she pleads for her life and her people, naming Haman as the adversary. The king storms out in anger; Haman falls on Esther's couch to beg, and the king returns, interprets it as an assault, and orders Haman hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai.

segments.title: Esther's plea at the banquet
segments.gist: At the second banquet, the king asks Esther's petition, and she asks for her life and her people's lives.

segments.title: Esther identifies Haman
segments.gist: Esther names Haman as the adversary and enemy, and Haman is terrified before the king and queen.

segments.title: King's anger and Haman's fall
segments.gist: The king storms out in anger; Haman pleads with Esther, and the king returns to find him fallen on her couch.

segments.title: Haman hanged on his gallows
segments.gist: Harbonah mentions the gallows Haman built for Mordecai, and the king orders Haman hanged there; the king's wrath is pacified.

8.summary: King Ahasuerus gives Esther the house of Haman and grants her and Mordecai authority to counter the decree against the Jews. Mordecai dictates a new decree in the king's name allowing the Jews to defend themselves, and the city of Shushan rejoices while many people become Jews.

segments.title: Esther Receives Haman's House
segments.gist: The king gives Esther Haman's estate, and she sets Mordecai over it after revealing their relationship.

segments.title: Esther Pleads to Reverse Decree
segments.gist: Esther asks the king to revoke the letters devised by Haman against the Jews, and he authorizes a new decree.

segments.title: Mordecai Writes New Decree
segments.gist: Mordecai dictates a decree in the king's name permitting Jews to defend themselves, sent by couriers throughout the provinces.

segments.title: Decree Allows Jewish Self-Defense
segments.gist: The decree grants Jews in every city the right to gather and defend themselves against any attackers.

segments.title: Mordecai Exalted and Jews Rejoice
segments.gist: Mordecai leaves the king's presence in royal apparel, and the Jews celebrate with joy while many become Jews.

9.summary: The Jews assemble and defend themselves, killing their enemies throughout the provinces, including the ten sons of Haman in Shushan. Esther asks for a second day of fighting in Shushan, and the Jews there hang Haman's sons and kill more enemies. The chapter then records the establishment of the feast of Purim to commemorate the deliverance.

segments.title: Jews Defend Themselves
segments.gist: On the appointed day, the Jews gather to defend themselves and kill those who sought their harm, including Haman's ten sons.

segments.title: Second Day in Shushan
segments.gist: Esther requests another day of fighting in Shushan, and the king grants it; the Jews kill three hundred more men and hang Haman's sons.

segments.title: Jews Slay Enemies in Provinces
segments.gist: The Jews in the provinces kill seventy-five thousand enemies and rest on the fourteenth day, while those in Shushan rest on the fifteenth.

segments.title: Feast of Purim Established
segments.gist: Mordecai writes letters to all the Jews, establishing an annual feast on the fourteenth and fifteenth days to remember their deliverance.

segments.title: Esther Confirms Purim
segments.gist: Queen Esther and Mordecai send a second letter with authority to confirm the observance of Purim among the Jews.

10.summary: King Ahasuerus imposes a tribute on the land and the isles, and the record of Mordecai's greatness is written in the chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia. Mordecai the Jew, second only to the king, is praised for seeking the welfare of his people and speaking peace to all his seed.

1.summary: Job, a wealthy and upright man in Uz, loses his children, servants, and livestock in a series of disasters, then his health, as Satan challenges his piety before God. Job responds with grief and worship, refusing to curse God.

segments.title: Job's Character and Prosperity
segments.gist: Job is introduced as blameless and wealthy, with seven sons, three daughters, and vast livestock.

segments.title: Satan's Challenge
segments.gist: God asks Satan about Job; Satan claims Job fears God only for blessings and asks to test him.

segments.title: Job Loses Children and Wealth
segments.gist: Messengers report the loss of oxen, sheep, camels, servants, and all of Job's children in a windstorm.

segments.title: Job's Grief and Worship
segments.gist: Job mourns, shaves his head, falls to the ground, and blesses God, saying he came naked and will return naked.

2.summary: Satan again appears before God and is permitted to afflict Job's body with boils, which Job endures while sitting among ashes. Job's wife urges him to curse God and die, but he refuses, and three friends arrive to mourn with him in silence for seven days.

segments.title: Satan permitted to afflict Job's body
segments.gist: God points to Job's integrity, and Satan claims a man will give all for his life; God allows Satan to touch Job's bone and flesh but spare his life.

segments.title: Job struck with boils
segments.gist: Satan smites Job with painful boils from head to foot, and Job sits among ashes scraping himself with a potsherd.

segments.title: Job's wife urges cursing God
segments.gist: Job's wife tells him to curse God and die, but Job replies that he should accept good and evil from God and does not sin with his lips.

segments.title: Three friends arrive to mourn
segments.gist: Three friends come to comfort Job, weep, tear their clothes, and sit with him on the ground for seven days without speaking.

3.summary: Job breaks his seven-day silence and curses the day he was born, wishing he had died at birth and questioning why light and life are given to those who suffer. He ends by lamenting that he has no peace, only turmoil.

segments.title: Job speaks and curses his birth
segments.gist: After seven days of silence, Job opens his mouth and curses the day of his birth.

segments.title: Job curses the day and night
segments.gist: Job calls for the day of his birth and the night of his conception to be blotted out and never counted.

segments.title: Why did I not die at birth?
segments.gist: Job asks why he did not die at birth, when the wicked and the weary alike find rest in the grave.

segments.title: Why is light given to the miserable?
segments.gist: Job questions why light and life are given to those in misery who long for death.

segments.title: Job's fear and lack of peace
segments.gist: Job says his worst fears have come upon him, and he has no peace, only trouble.

4.summary: Eliphaz, the first of Job's friends to speak, answers Job by recalling a night vision and arguing that no one innocent ever perished. He claims that suffering is the lot of those who sow trouble, and urges Job to seek God, who disciplines and heals.

segments.title: Eliphaz recalls Job's past counsel
segments.gist: Eliphaz asks if he may speak, reminds Job that he once strengthened the weak, and notes that trouble now falls on him.

segments.title: The innocent are not destroyed
segments.gist: Eliphaz asks who ever perished being innocent, and says the wicked are cut off like lions' whelps.

segments.title: Eliphaz's night vision
segments.gist: Eliphaz describes a fearful night vision in which a spirit asked whether mortal man can be more just or pure than God, who charges even angels with folly.

5.summary: Eliphaz continues his first speech to Job, arguing that suffering is the result of folly and that God disciplines those who turn to Him. He urges Job to seek God, who does great and unsearchable things, and promises restoration and protection for the one who accepts correction.

segments.title: Call to Seek God
segments.gist: Eliphaz invites Job to call upon God and argues that the foolish and envious are cut off, while the one who seeks God finds help.

segments.title: God's Great and Unsearchable Works
segments.gist: Eliphaz describes God's mighty acts in nature and His care for the humble, frustrating the plans of the crafty and saving the poor.

segments.title: Blessing of Divine Correction
segments.gist: Eliphaz declares that the man whom God corrects is blessed, promising protection, peace, and restoration for those who accept discipline.

6.summary: Job answers Eliphaz, insisting his complaint is justified because his suffering outweighs the sands of the sea. He longs for God to crush him and end his life, then rebukes his friends for failing to show kindness, comparing them to a dried-up brook that disappoints travelers. He appeals for them to teach him if he is wrong and laments that he has no strength or hope left.

segments.title: Job Defends His Complaint
segments.gist: Job says his grief is heavier than the sand, and the arrows of the Almighty have poisoned his spirit.

segments.title: Job Longs for Death
segments.gist: Job asks God to crush him and cut him off, preferring death over his unrelenting pain.

segments.title: Friends Compared to a Dry Brook
segments.gist: Job rebukes his friends for failing to show kindness, comparing them to a brook that dries up when travelers need it.

segments.title: Job Appeals for Honest Teaching
segments.gist: Job asks his friends to teach him if he is wrong, and laments that he has no strength or hope left.

7.summary: Job continues his reply to Eliphaz, describing human life as hard service and his own suffering as relentless, with no rest and no hope. He turns directly to God, accusing him of watching him, terrifying him with dreams, and refusing to pardon his sin, so that he longs for death.

segments.title: Life as Hard Service
segments.gist: Job compares human life to hired labor and slavery, longing for rest and shade but finding only months of misery and nights of weariness.

segments.title: Life Flees Without Hope
segments.gist: Job says his life is a breath and will soon be gone, with no return from the grave and no one to remember him.

segments.title: Job Will Not Restrain His Complaint
segments.gist: Job resolves to speak out in his anguish, accusing God of terrifying him with dreams and visions so that he prefers death to life.

segments.title: Why Does God Watch Man?
segments.gist: Job asks why God pays such close attention to him, testing him every moment, and demands why God will not pardon his sin or leave him alone.

8.summary: Bildad the Shuhite answers Job, arguing that God is just and that Job's suffering must be due to his or his children's sin. He appeals to tradition and nature, urging Job to repent and promising restoration if he does.

segments.title: Bildad Rebukes Job's Words
segments.gist: Bildad asks how long Job will speak such things and insists that God does not pervert justice, implying Job's children died for their sins.

segments.title: Appeal to Ancient Tradition
segments.gist: Bildad urges Job to inquire of past generations and learn from the wisdom of the fathers.

segments.title: Lessons from Nature
segments.gist: Bildad compares the godless to papyrus and a spider's web, which wither and are forgotten without God's support.

segments.title: Promise of Restoration
segments.gist: Bildad assures Job that God will not cast away a blameless man but will fill his mouth with laughter and restore him.

9.summary: Job answers Bildad, agreeing that God is wise and mighty but questioning how a mortal can be just before him. He describes God's power over nature and his own inability to plead his case, lamenting that God seems to treat him as an enemy despite his integrity.

segments.title: Job Acknowledges God's Justice
segments.gist: Job agrees that God is just and asks how a man can be righteous before God, who is infinitely wise.

segments.title: God's Power Over Creation
segments.gist: Job describes God's mighty acts: moving mountains, shaking the earth, commanding the sun, and controlling the seas.

segments.title: Job's Inability to Plead
segments.gist: Job says he cannot answer God or choose words before him; even if righteous, he would be condemned by God's power.

segments.title: Job's Complaint of Injustice
segments.gist: Job claims he is blameless yet despises his life; he says God destroys both perfect and wicked, and mocks the innocent.

segments.title: Days Flee Without Hope
segments.gist: Job laments that his days are swift and without hope; even washing with snow would leave him filthy.

segments.title: No Mediator Between Job and God
segments.gist: Job wishes for a daysman to mediate, but says God is not a man like him, so he cannot answer without fear.

10.summary: Job continues his complaint to God, expressing weariness of life and asking God to show him why he is being afflicted. He pleads for a reprieve, questioning whether his few days of life can be spared before he goes to the grave.

segments.title: Job's Complaint and Plea
segments.gist: Job expresses loathing for his life and asks God to reveal the reason for His contention, questioning if it pleases God to oppress him.

segments.title: God's Care and Job's Suffering
segments.gist: Job acknowledges God's hands formed him, yet feels God now destroys him and shows relentless hostility, leaving him no respite.

segments.title: Job's Plea for Respite
segments.gist: Job asks why he was born and begs for a few days of relief before he dies and enters the land of darkness.

11.summary: Zophar the Naamathite answers Job, accusing him of empty talk and claiming that God's wisdom is unsearchable and that Job is receiving less than his iniquity deserves. He urges Job to repent and promises restoration if he puts away sin, describing the security and hope that would follow.

segments.title: Zophar Rebukes Job's Words
segments.gist: Zophar asks if a man full of talk should be justified and wishes God would speak against Job's claims.

segments.title: God's Wisdom Is Unsearchable
segments.gist: Zophar declares God's wisdom and power beyond human understanding, describing his sovereign rule over men.

segments.title: Call to Repent and Be Restored
segments.gist: Zophar urges Job to set his heart right and put away iniquity, promising security, brightness, and hope.

12.summary: Job answers his friends with sharp irony, claiming he knows as much as they do and that their prosperity has made them smug. He then turns to creation and to God's unsearchable power, declaring that wisdom and might belong to God alone, who overturns counselors, judges, and mighty men.

segments.title: Job's Irony Toward Friends
segments.gist: Job sarcastically says wisdom will die with his friends, yet he understands as much as they do and is mocked despite his integrity.

segments.title: Creation and God's Wisdom
segments.gist: Job appeals to beasts, birds, and fish to show that God's hand gives life and breath, and that wisdom and understanding belong to Him.

segments.title: God's Power Over the Mighty
segments.gist: Job describes God's sovereign power to overturn counselors, judges, kings, priests, and nations, bringing darkness and confusion.

13.summary: Job answers his friends, calling them worthless physicians and accusing them of speaking falsely for God. He declares his resolve to argue his case directly with God, even at the risk of his life, and laments the severity of his suffering while pleading for a hearing and a fair chance to speak.

segments.title: Job rebukes his friends
segments.gist: Job calls his friends worthless physicians and accuses them of speaking deceitfully for God, warning that God will reprove their partiality.

segments.title: Job resolves to speak to God
segments.gist: Job declares he will speak boldly and argue his case with God, trusting in his own integrity and expecting to be vindicated.

segments.title: Job pleads for relief and answers
segments.gist: Job asks God for two things: to withdraw his hand and not terrify him, then lists his sins and laments his suffering and isolation.

14.summary: Job continues his reply to Zophar, lamenting the brevity and hardship of human life, contrasting humanity's fleeting days with the hope of a tree that sprouts again when cut. He longs for death to hide him until God's wrath passes and asks whether a man can live again, then describes the erosion of hope by suffering and the finality of death.

segments.title: Job Laments Human Frailty
segments.gist: Job describes man's brief, trouble-filled life and asks God to look away and let him rest.

segments.title: Hope of a Tree vs. Man
segments.gist: Job contrasts a tree that sprouts again when cut with man who dies and lies down, not rising until the heavens are no more.

segments.title: Longing for Hidden Rest
segments.gist: Job wishes to be hidden in the grave until God's wrath passes, asking for a set time and a release from his present suffering.

segments.title: Erosion of Hope
segments.gist: Job compares hope to a mountain that falls and crumbles, and to water that wears away stones, concluding that God destroys man's hope and he feels only his own pain.

15.summary: Eliphaz the Temanite answers Job a second time, accusing him of empty talk and of undermining reverence for God. He appeals to the wisdom of the ancients, describes the misery of the wicked who defy God, and warns Job that his own words condemn him.

segments.title: Eliphaz Rebukes Job's Words
segments.gist: Eliphaz accuses Job of answering with vain knowledge and says his own mouth condemns him.

segments.title: Job's Presumption and Human Corruption
segments.gist: Eliphaz asks if Job was the first man born and insists that no one born of woman can be pure before God.

segments.title: The Fate of the Wicked
segments.gist: Eliphaz describes the troubles that come upon the wicked, who stretch out their hand against God and trust in vanity.

16.summary: Job answers Eliphaz, calling his friends miserable comforters whose words bring no relief. He describes his suffering as God's assault, yet he appeals to the earth and to a heavenly witness to plead his case, and affirms his hope that his cry will be heard.

segments.title: Job Rebukes His Friends
segments.gist: Job calls his friends miserable comforters and says he could speak as they do if they were in his place.

segments.title: Job Describes God's Assault
segments.gist: Job says his grief is not lessened, and describes God as having torn him and broken him with repeated attacks.

segments.title: Job's Mourning and Innocence
segments.gist: Job wears sackcloth, his face is foul with weeping, and he protests that his hands are free from violence and his prayer is pure.

segments.title: Job Appeals to a Heavenly Witness
segments.gist: Job calls on the earth not to cover his blood and asks for a witness in heaven to plead with God on his behalf.

17.summary: Job continues his reply to Eliphaz, lamenting that his spirit is broken, his days are extinct, and the grave is ready for him. He protests that mockers surround him and that God has made him a byword, while he clings to the hope that the upright will be astonished and the innocent will hold his way. He challenges his friends to return and find no wisdom in him, then describes death as a hopeless descent to the pit.

segments.title: Job's broken spirit
segments.gist: Job declares his spirit is broken, his days are extinct, and the grave is ready for him.

segments.title: Mockers and God's hand
segments.gist: Job complains that mockers surround him and that God has made him a byword and a target.

segments.title: Hope for the upright
segments.gist: Job describes his grief but affirms that the righteous will hold their way and the innocent will grow stronger.

segments.title: Challenge to friends
segments.gist: Job challenges his friends to return, asserting that no wise man is among them and that his plans are broken.

segments.title: Descent to the grave
segments.gist: Job speaks of the grave as his only hope and home, asking where his hope and rest have gone.

18.summary: Bildad the Shuhite answers Job, rebuking him for treating his friends as beasts and insisting that the wicked are always punished. He describes the terrors, losses, and death that overtake the wicked and their families.

segments.title: Bildad Rebukes Job's Words
segments.gist: Bildad asks how long Job will speak and why he counts his friends as beasts and unclean.

segments.title: The Wicked's Light Extinguished
segments.gist: Bildad declares that the light of the wicked is put out and his own counsel casts him down.

segments.title: Terrors and Calamity
segments.gist: Terrors frighten the wicked, his strength is wasted, and calamity waits at his side.

segments.title: Root and Branch Withered
segments.gist: The wicked's roots and branches dry up, his memory perishes, and he has no offspring among his people.

19.summary: Job answers Bildad, complaining that his friends have become his tormentors and that God has broken him down. He cries out for pity, laments that his family and servants have turned from him, and declares his confidence that his Redeemer lives and will vindicate him in the end.

segments.title: Job Feels Wronged by God
segments.gist: Job complains that his friends reproach him and that God has broken him down with his net, crying out for help but finding no answer.

segments.title: God Has Stripped Job's Honor
segments.gist: Job says God has fenced him in, stripped him of glory, and treats him as an enemy, sending troops against him.

segments.title: Family and Friends Have Turned Away
segments.gist: Job laments that his relatives, servants, and close friends have forsaken him, and even his wife and children regard him as a stranger.

segments.title: Job Pleads for Pity
segments.gist: Job begs his friends to have pity on him because the hand of God has touched him, asking why they persecute him further.

segments.title: Job's Hope in a Living Redeemer
segments.gist: Job longs for his words to be recorded and declares his confidence that his Redeemer lives and will stand on the earth, and that he will see God in his flesh.

20.summary: Zophar the Naamathite answers Job a second time, declaring that the triumph of the wicked is brief and that his prosperity quickly perishes. He describes the wicked man's downfall, the loss of his wealth, and the certainty of God's judgment upon him and his family.

segments.title: Zophar: Wicked's Joy Is Brief
segments.gist: Zophar asserts that the wicked's exaltation is short-lived and that he will perish forever like his own dung.

segments.title: Wicked's Sweetness Turns to Bitterness
segments.gist: Though wickedness is sweet in his mouth, it becomes poison within him; he will not enjoy the wealth he gained by oppressing the poor.

segments.title: Wicked's Destruction and God's Wrath
segments.gist: Because he knew no quietness, the wicked will face God's fierce wrath; his house and possessions will be utterly consumed.

21.summary: Job answers Zophar's claim that the wicked are swiftly punished, arguing from experience that the wicked often prosper, live long, and die in peace, and he asks why the wicked are not judged openly. He dismisses his friends' empty comfort as false and challenges them to show him any real evidence of his own sin.

segments.title: Job asks to be heard
segments.gist: Job invites his friends to listen carefully, then protests that their consolation is vain and false.

segments.title: The wicked prosper
segments.gist: Job observes that the wicked live, grow old, have large households, and enjoy prosperity, seemingly untouched by God's rod.

segments.title: How often are they judged?
segments.gist: Job asks how often the wicked are punished, noting that they often die in peace and ask who God is.

segments.title: God judges the high
segments.gist: Job questions whether anyone can teach God knowledge, noting that one dies in prosperity and another in bitterness.

segments.title: Job rejects false comfort
segments.gist: Job knows his friends' thoughts and denies their claim that the wicked are always punished, calling their answers false.

22.summary: Eliphaz the Temanite delivers his third speech to Job, accusing him of great wickedness and listing specific sins he claims Job has committed. He argues that Job's suffering is God's just punishment and calls Job to repent and be restored, promising prosperity if he returns to the Almighty.

segments.title: Eliphaz Questions Job's Righteousness
segments.gist: Eliphaz asks if a man can be profitable to God and suggests Job's fear of God is not the reason for his suffering.

segments.title: Accusation of Specific Sins
segments.gist: Eliphaz accuses Job of taking pledges from the poor, withholding bread and water, and oppressing widows and orphans.

segments.title: God's Judgment on the Wicked
segments.gist: Eliphaz describes God's lofty perspective and declares that the wicked are cut off, implying Job should heed this warning.

segments.title: Call to Repentance and Restoration
segments.gist: Eliphaz urges Job to acquaint himself with God, put away iniquity, and promises that God will hear and restore him.

23.summary: Job answers Eliphaz, expressing a longing to find God and present his case directly, but he cannot locate Him. He affirms God's sovereign power and his own integrity, yet is terrified by God's hidden purposes and the darkness that surrounds him.

segments.title: Job longs to find God
segments.gist: Job complains that his groaning is bitter and wishes he could find God to lay his case before Him, confident he would be heard.

segments.title: God is hidden but knows Job's way
segments.gist: Job cannot find God on any side, yet trusts that God knows his path and that he will come forth as gold because he has kept God's commandments.

segments.title: Job fears God's hidden purpose
segments.gist: Job acknowledges God's unchanging will and is terrified by His presence, feeling that darkness and thick clouds cover him.

24.summary: Job continues his reply, arguing that the wicked often go unpunished and that God seems indifferent to injustice. He describes specific crimes—moving boundary stones, oppressing the poor, murder, adultery, and theft—and notes that these wrongdoers often die in peace, while others suffer. Job challenges the idea that God swiftly judges the wicked, pointing to the prosperity and security many evildoers enjoy.

segments.title: Job Laments God's Unseen Judgment
segments.gist: Job asks why God does not set times of judgment and complains that the wicked remove landmarks and seize flocks.

segments.title: The Poor Are Oppressed
segments.gist: Job describes the poor being driven from their homes, laboring without food or clothing, and dying while God does not intervene.

segments.title: Sinners of the Night
segments.gist: Job portrays murderers, adulterers, and thieves who work under cover of darkness, showing their rebellion against the light.

segments.title: The Wicked's Swift End
segments.gist: Job acknowledges that the wicked may be swiftly swept away, cursed, and forgotten, with no lasting legacy.

segments.title: God's Mysterious Ways
segments.gist: Job concludes that God may let the wicked prosper and then bring sudden terror, and he challenges anyone to prove him wrong.

25.summary: Bildad the Shuhite gives his third and shortest speech, answering Job by exalting God's absolute dominion and purity. He asks how any mortal can be righteous before God, since even the moon and stars are not pure in His sight, and concludes that man, a worm, is far less so.

segments.title: Bildad exalts God's dominion
segments.gist: Bildad declares that dominion and fear belong to God, who makes peace in His high places and commands countless armies.

segments.title: Man's impurity before God
segments.gist: Bildad asks how a man born of a woman can be righteous or clean before God, who charges even the moon and stars with impurity.

26.summary: Job answers Bildad with sharp sarcasm, mocking his friend's counsel as unhelpful and powerless. He then contrasts human weakness with God's vast dominion over the dead, the earth, the waters, and the heavens, declaring that what people hear of God is only a whisper of his true power.

segments.title: Job Mocks Bildad's Help
segments.gist: Job sarcastically asks how Bildad has helped the weak and powerless with his counsel.

segments.title: God's Power Over the Dead
segments.gist: Job describes the dead trembling beneath the waters and Sheol lying naked before God.

segments.title: God Stretches the Heavens
segments.gist: Job tells how God spreads the north over empty space, binds the waters, and sets bounds on light and darkness.

segments.title: God Stills the Sea
segments.gist: Job says the pillars of heaven tremble, God stills the sea, and his Spirit garnished the heavens.

27.summary: Job continues his final reply, insisting on his integrity and refusing to concede that he is wicked. He describes the fate that awaits the wicked, even as he acknowledges that their prosperity and downfall lie in God's hands.

segments.title: Job Maintains His Integrity
segments.gist: Job vows to hold fast to his righteousness and refuses to accept his friends' claim that he is wicked.

segments.title: Job Describes the Wicked's Hope
segments.gist: Job asks what hope the hypocrite has when God takes away his soul, noting that God will not hear his cry.

segments.title: Job Describes the Wicked's Portion
segments.gist: Job declares the inheritance the wicked receive from God: their children perish, they gather wealth but lose it, and terrors overtake them.

28.summary: Job describes the arduous human search for wisdom, contrasting it with the hidden treasures of the earth that people dig for. He declares that wisdom cannot be bought with gold or precious stones, and that only God knows its place, having established it and declared that the fear of the Lord is wisdom.

segments.title: Human Mining for Treasure
segments.gist: People dig deep into the earth for silver, gold, iron, and precious stones, bringing hidden things to light.

segments.title: Wisdom's Inaccessibility
segments.gist: Wisdom cannot be found in the land of the living nor bought with gold, silver, or precious stones.

segments.title: God Alone Knows Wisdom
segments.gist: Wisdom is hidden from all living creatures, but God understands its place and declares that fearing the Lord is wisdom.

29.summary: Job continues his final speech by recalling his former prosperity and honor, when God's favor seemed to rest on him and he was respected at the city gate. He describes his past role as a protector of the poor and a judge whose counsel was valued, contrasting that standing with his present suffering.

segments.title: Job Longs for Former Days
segments.gist: Job expresses longing for the months when God's favor and intimate friendship seemed to surround him and his household.

segments.title: Respected at the City Gate
segments.gist: Job recalls how young men and elders alike would rise and stand in respect when he appeared at the city gate.

segments.title: Advocate for the Poor
segments.gist: Job describes his past deeds of delivering the poor, the fatherless, the blind, the lame, and the needy from oppression.

segments.title: Expected Continued Prosperity
segments.gist: Job says he thought he would die in his nest, with his root spread out and his glory fresh and his bow renewed.

segments.title: Counsel Like Rain and Dew
segments.gist: Job recalls how people waited for his advice and accepted it like rain and dew, and he sat as a leader and comforter among them.

30.summary: Job continues his final speech, contrasting his former honor and prosperity with his present humiliation and suffering. He describes being mocked by outcasts and afflicted by God, and he cries out to God for help but receives no answer, ending in mourning and desolation.

segments.title: Job recalls former honor
segments.gist: Job remembers when God preserved him and young men and princes showed him respect.

segments.title: Mocked by base men
segments.gist: Job laments that he is now mocked by outcasts and despised, with his dignity swept away.

segments.title: Afflicted by God
segments.gist: Job describes his inner turmoil and God's harsh treatment, casting him into the mire.

segments.title: Cry unanswered, mourning
segments.gist: Job cries out to God but receives no answer; he mourns in desolation and darkness.

31.summary: Job continues his final defense, declaring his integrity before God by listing the sins he has avoided—such as lust, deceit, injustice, and idolatry—and the calamities he would deserve if guilty. He protests his innocence and calls for God to answer him, insisting that his words are true and his cause just.

segments.title: Job's covenant with his eyes
segments.gist: Job declares he has made a covenant not to look lustfully at a virgin and asks what portion God allots to the wicked.

segments.title: Job denies deceit and falsehood
segments.gist: Job asserts he has not walked with vanity or deceit, and calls for God to weigh him and know his integrity.

segments.title: Job denies adultery
segments.gist: Job says he has not been enticed by a neighbor's wife, for that would be a heinous crime deserving destruction.

segments.title: Job's justice toward servants and poor
segments.gist: Job recounts his fair treatment of servants and his care for the poor, widow, and fatherless, fearing God's judgment.

segments.title: Job denies trust in wealth and idols
segments.gist: Job says he has not made gold his hope or kissed his hand to idols, which would be a denial of God.

segments.title: Job denies revenge and hypocrisy
segments.gist: Job claims he has not rejoiced at his enemy's downfall, nor hidden sin, nor feared public opinion.

segments.title: Job calls for God's answer
segments.gist: Job longs for God to hear him, signs his defense, and challenges his adversary, confident in his integrity.

32.summary: Job's three friends stop answering him, and the younger Elihu, angry that Job justified himself rather than God and that the friends had failed to refute him, speaks up after waiting out of respect for their age. He declares he will now give his own answer, insisting that wisdom comes from God's spirit rather than from age alone.

segments.title: Elihu's anger kindles
segments.gist: Because the three friends cease answering Job, Elihu the Buzite becomes angry at Job for justifying himself and at the friends for condemning him without proof.

segments.title: Elihu explains his delay
segments.gist: Elihu says he held back out of respect for age, but declares that it is the spirit of God, not mere years, that gives understanding.

segments.title: Elihu rejects their arguments
segments.gist: Elihu says he waited for their reasoning but found none of them could refute Job; he will not use their arguments.

segments.title: Elihu resolves to speak
segments.gist: Seeing the friends dismayed and silent, Elihu says he is full of words and will speak without partiality, not flattering any man.

33.summary: Elihu continues his speech, addressing Job directly: he claims to speak with sincerity and God-given spirit, challenges Job's complaint that God is silent and unjust, and explains that God speaks through dreams, pain, and a mediator to turn a person back from destruction and restore them.

segments.title: Elihu invites Job to hear
segments.gist: Elihu calls Job to listen, declares his words are upright and sincere, and says he is formed from clay like Job, so Job need not fear him.

segments.title: Job's claim of innocence
segments.gist: Elihu quotes Job's assertion that he is pure and without sin, and answers that God is greater than man and not accountable to human standards.

segments.title: God speaks through dreams and pain
segments.gist: Elihu explains that God speaks in dreams and visions to warn people, and also through pain on the bed to turn them from pride and destruction.

segments.title: Affliction and approaching death
segments.gist: Elihu describes a person chastened with pain, unable to eat, wasting away, drawing near to the grave and destruction.

segments.title: A mediator brings restoration
segments.gist: If a messenger or mediator intercedes, declaring what is right, the person is spared from the pit and their flesh is restored like a child's; they pray and God delivers them.

segments.title: God's repeated dealings with man
segments.gist: Elihu concludes that God does all these things repeatedly to turn a person from destruction and give them light, and urges Job to listen and speak if he has anything to say.

34.summary: Elihu continues his speech, addressing Job's claim that God is unjust and that he has no profit from righteousness. Elihu argues that God is just and sovereign, repays each according to his deeds, and that Job speaks without knowledge, adding rebellion to his sin.

segments.title: Elihu addresses the wise
segments.gist: Elihu calls on the wise and knowledgeable to listen and test his words, for the ear discerns words as the palate tastes food.

segments.title: Job's claim of injustice
segments.gist: Elihu quotes Job's assertion that he is righteous but God has wronged him, and that he is wounded without cause.

segments.title: God is just and sovereign
segments.gist: Elihu insists that God is far from wickedness and that as sovereign Creator He can do as He pleases with all flesh.

segments.title: God's impartial judgment
segments.gist: Elihu argues that God, who judges without partiality, is not accountable to any man and can overturn rulers in a moment.

segments.title: God sees all and judges
segments.gist: Elihu declares that God sees every step of man and judges the mighty without inquiry, especially the hypocrites who oppress others.

segments.title: Job's words lack knowledge
segments.gist: Elihu challenges Job to repent and cease speaking without knowledge, accusing him of adding rebellion to his sin.

35.summary: Elihu continues his speech, addressing Job's claim that he is more righteous than God and that his righteousness profits him nothing. Elihu argues that human sin or righteousness does not affect God Himself but only other people, and that God does not answer the proud when they cry out. He concludes that Job speaks without knowledge and should be tested further for his rebellious answers.

segments.title: Elihu Addresses Job's Claim
segments.gist: Elihu questions Job's assertion that his righteousness exceeds God's and that he gains nothing from not sinning.

segments.title: Sin and Righteousness Affect Others
segments.gist: Elihu argues that human wickedness or righteousness impacts other people, not God in heaven.

segments.title: Why God Does Not Answer
segments.gist: Elihu says the oppressed cry out but God does not answer because of pride, and they fail to seek their Maker.

segments.title: Job's Empty Words
segments.gist: Elihu concludes that God does not hear empty cries, and Job speaks without knowledge, multiplying words.

36.summary: Elihu continues his speech, asserting that God is just and uses suffering to discipline and instruct people, and that those who respond rightly are restored while the rebellious perish. He then describes God's greatness in nature—rain, clouds, lightning, and thunder—as beyond human understanding, and calls Job to consider God's majesty rather than accuse him.

segments.title: Elihu Claims God's Justice
segments.gist: Elihu asks Job to listen, promising to show that God is mighty and just, and does not despise anyone.

segments.title: Suffering as Divine Discipline
segments.gist: Elihu says God uses affliction to open people's ears and warn them, and those who respond are restored.

segments.title: Fate of the Godless
segments.gist: Elihu contrasts the godless who perish in anger with Job, whom he says God is drawing from distress to abundance.

segments.title: Warning Against Choosing Iniquity
segments.gist: Elihu warns Job not to turn to iniquity or wealth, and to avoid the fate of the wicked.

segments.title: God's Greatness in Nature
segments.gist: Elihu calls Job to exalt God's work and declares that God is great beyond human understanding.

segments.title: Rain, Clouds, and Thunder
segments.gist: Elihu describes how God draws up water, spreads clouds, and sends lightning and thunder as signs of his majesty.

37.summary: Elihu concludes his speech, describing God's thunder, lightning, snow, and winds as instruments of His voice and judgment. He challenges Job to explain how God orders the clouds and light, and declares God's majesty too great for human comprehension, warning that men should fear Him.

segments.title: God's Voice in Nature
segments.gist: Elihu describes thunder, lightning, snow, and rain as God's voice and instruments of judgment or mercy.

segments.title: Job Challenged to Explain
segments.gist: Elihu challenges Job to explain how God orders the clouds and spreads the sky like a mirror.

segments.title: God's Majesty and Fear
segments.gist: Elihu says God's majesty is beyond human reach and that men should fear Him.

38.summary: The LORD answers Job out of a whirlwind, challenging him to explain the foundations of the earth, the ordering of the heavens, and the provision for wild creatures, thereby asserting divine wisdom and power over creation.

segments.title: The LORD speaks from the whirlwind
segments.gist: The LORD answers Job out of a whirlwind, questioning who darkens counsel with words without knowledge and calling Job to stand and answer.

segments.title: Where wast thou at creation?
segments.gist: The LORD asks where Job was when the foundations of the earth were laid, when the morning stars sang and the sons of God shouted for joy.

segments.title: Questions about the deep and light
segments.gist: The LORD questions Job about the springs of the sea, the gates of death, the breadth of the earth, and the dwelling place of light and darkness.

segments.title: Who orders the rain and ice?
segments.gist: The LORD asks who divides the watercourse for rain, sends lightning, and brings forth ice and frost from the womb.

segments.title: Canst thou bind the constellations?
segments.gist: The LORD challenges Job to bind the sweet influences of Pleiades, loose Orion, and guide the stars, and to know the ordinances of heaven.

segments.title: Who provides for the creatures?
segments.gist: The LORD asks who gives understanding to the heart, provides prey for the lion and raven, and knows the times of the wild goats and hinds.

39.summary: God continues his speech to Job, turning to the animal world: wild goats and deer, the wild donkey, the ostrich, the horse, and the hawk and eagle. He asks Job whether he can explain or control these creatures, pressing Job to answer the one who made them.

segments.title: Wild Goats and Hinds
segments.gist: God asks Job if he knows when wild goats and hinds give birth and how their young grow.

segments.title: The Free Wild Donkey
segments.gist: God describes the wild donkey he has set free to live in the wilderness, scorning the city.

segments.title: The Unruly Wild Ox
segments.gist: God asks whether the wild ox will serve Job, plow his fields, or be trusted to bring in his harvest.

segments.title: The Ostrich's Strange Ways
segments.gist: God describes the ostrich, which leaves its eggs on the ground and lacks wisdom, yet outruns the horse.

segments.title: The War Horse
segments.gist: God describes the horse's strength and courage in battle, unafraid of sword or spear.

segments.title: Hawk and Eagle
segments.gist: God asks if Job commands the hawk's flight and describes the eagle nesting on high and feeding its young on blood.

40.summary: The chapter continues God's answer to Job out of the whirlwind. God challenges Job to match His power and justice, then points him to Behemoth as a display of divine strength that no human can tame.

segments.title: God Challenges Job to Answer
segments.gist: The LORD asks Job whether he will still contend with the Almighty and rebuke Him; Job replies that he is vile and will say no more.

segments.title: God Dares Job to Show Power
segments.gist: God challenges Job to clothe himself with majesty and glory, pour out his wrath, and humble the proud, and then God will acknowledge him.

segments.title: Behemoth Described as God's Creature
segments.gist: God describes Behemoth, which eats grass like an ox and has strength in its loins, and says no one can approach it with a sword or capture it.

41.summary: God continues his speech to Job, describing the great sea creature Leviathan, which no human can capture or tame. He challenges Job to match his power over such a beast, declaring that only God can subdue it and that all under heaven belongs to him.

segments.title: God challenges Job to catch Leviathan
segments.gist: God asks if Job can draw out Leviathan with a hook or tame it, and warns against laying hands on it.

segments.title: No one dares stir up Leviathan
segments.gist: God declares that no one is fierce enough to rouse Leviathan, and that everything under heaven belongs to him.

segments.title: Description of Leviathan's body
segments.gist: God describes Leviathan's powerful limbs, impenetrable scales, flaming breath, and smoke from its nostrils.

segments.title: Leviathan's terror and strength
segments.gist: God tells how Leviathan terrifies the mighty, has a strong heart, and makes the deep boil, with no equal on earth.

42.summary: Job answers the LORD, admitting he spoke of things he did not understand and repenting in dust and ashes. The LORD then rebukes Eliphaz and his two friends, requiring them to offer a burnt offering and have Job pray for them. After Job prays, the LORD restores his fortunes, giving him double what he had before, and blesses his latter days with wealth, family, and a long life.

segments.title: Job's confession and repentance
segments.gist: Job acknowledges God's power, admits he spoke without understanding, and repents in dust and ashes.

segments.title: God rebukes the three friends
segments.gist: The LORD tells Eliphaz that he and his friends have not spoken rightly, and requires a burnt offering and Job's prayer.

segments.title: Job prays and is restored
segments.gist: Job prays for his friends, and the LORD restores his fortunes, giving him double what he had before.

segments.title: Job's restored family and wealth
segments.gist: Job receives twice as many sheep, camels, oxen, and donkeys, and has seven sons and three daughters.

segments.title: Job's daughters and inheritance
segments.gist: Job names his three daughters and gives them an inheritance among their brothers.

1.summary: Psalm 1 contrasts the righteous, who delight in God's law and are like a fruitful tree by water, with the wicked, who are like chaff blown away and will not stand in judgment.

segments.title: The Righteous Described
segments.gist: The blessed man avoids the counsel of the ungodly and delights in the law of the Lord, meditating on it day and night.

segments.title: The Righteous Compared to a Tree
