segments.gist: A king's lips and wrath are described, and righteousness in leadership is valued.

segments.title: Wisdom and Humility Over Pride
segments.gist: Wisdom is better than gold, and humility precedes honor while pride precedes destruction.

segments.title: The Blessing of Wise Speech and Labor
segments.gist: Those who heed the word find good, and the laborer's appetite drives his work.

segments.title: The Destructive Ways of the Wicked
segments.gist: Ungodly men devise mischief, sow strife, and lead others into harm.

segments.title: Aging Righteously and God's Final Word
segments.gist: A hoary head is a crown of glory, and the lot is cast but its outcome is from the Lord.

17.summary: Proverbs 17 is a collection of wise sayings contrasting righteous and foolish behavior. It covers themes such as the value of peace, the testing of hearts by God, the consequences of gossip and bribery, and the importance of controlling one's tongue. The chapter also addresses family relationships, justice, and the danger of pride.

segments.title: Peace, testing, and evil
segments.gist: Better a dry morsel with quiet than a house full of feasting with strife; God tests hearts; the wicked and proud are condemned.

segments.title: Family and speech
segments.gist: Grandchildren are a crown; false speech and bribery distort justice; love covers offenses, but repeating a matter separates friends.

segments.title: Rebellion and strife
segments.gist: A rebuke affects the wise more than a hundred blows on a fool; evil people and false witnesses bring trouble; starting a quarrel is like releasing water.

segments.title: Folly and injustice
segments.gist: Justifying the wicked and condemning the righteous are both abominable; a fool has no wisdom to buy; a friend loves at all times; a man void of understanding pledges and becomes surety.

segments.title: Foolish children and justice
segments.gist: A foolish son brings grief; a cheerful heart is good medicine; the wicked take bribes to pervert justice; a wise man sets his face against evil.

segments.title: The value of silence
segments.gist: He who restrains his words has knowledge, and even a fool who keeps silent is considered wise.

18.summary: Proverbs 18 is a collection of wise sayings contrasting the foolish and the wise, covering topics such as isolation, speech, partiality, the power of the tongue, wealth, pride, and the value of a true friend. It emphasizes that words can bring life or death, that humility precedes honor, and that a faithful friend is a rare treasure.

segments.title: Foolishness, Speech, and Partiality
segments.gist: The chapter opens with sayings on the fool's isolation, the fool's lack of understanding, the power of words, and the injustice of favoring the wicked.

segments.title: The Name of the Lord and the Tongue
segments.gist: These verses contrast the security of the righteous in the Lord's name with the fool's ruin, and highlight the tongue's power to bring death or life.

segments.title: Wealth, Pride, and Disputes
segments.gist: Sayings address the influence of gifts, the danger of pride before honor, the folly of judging before hearing, and the difficulty of resolving quarrels.

segments.title: Words, Friends, and the Lord's Help
segments.gist: The chapter closes with sayings on the fruit of one's words, the power of the tongue, the need for the Lord's help, and the value of a true friend.

19.summary: Proverbs 19 is a collection of wise sayings contrasting integrity with folly, the value of a good wife, the consequences of laziness and false witness, and the fear of the Lord. It includes instructions on listening to counsel, caring for the poor, and disciplining children, ending with a warning about the rod and the hope of wisdom.

segments.title: Wealth, friends, and false witnesses
segments.gist: Contrasts the poor who walk in integrity with the rich who are perverse, and warns against false witnesses and the folly of anger.

segments.title: Wisdom, folly, and a prudent wife
segments.gist: Describes how wisdom brings favor, folly leads to ruin, and a prudent wife is from the Lord, while laziness brings poverty.

segments.title: Keeping commandments and helping the poor
segments.gist: Encourages keeping the commandments, giving to the poor, and listening to counsel, with the assurance that the Lord will repay kindness.

segments.title: The fear of the Lord and discipline
segments.gist: Highlights the fear of the Lord as leading to life, warns against laziness and falsehood, and advises disciplining a child while there is hope.

segments.title: Warnings against shameful children and false witnesses
segments.gist: Warns against children who shame their parents, false witnesses, and scoffers, ending with the certainty of judgment for the wicked.

20.summary: Proverbs 20 is a collection of Solomon's wise sayings on a range of topics, including the dangers of wine, the folly of quarreling, the value of honest labor, the importance of just weights and measures, and the consequences of laziness and deceit. It contrasts the righteous and the wicked, emphasizing that God sees all actions and that a person's character is revealed in their conduct.

segments.title: Avoid Strife and Sloth
segments.gist: The fear of a king is like a roaring lion; it is an honor to cease from strife, and the sluggard will not plow by reason of the cold.

segments.title: Counsel and Integrity
segments.gist: Counsel in the heart is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out; most men will proclaim their own goodness, but a faithful man who can find?

segments.title: Even a Child Is Known
segments.gist: Even a child is known by his doings; the hearing ear and the seeing eye are both made by the Lord; love not sleep lest thou come to poverty.

segments.title: Gold and Lips of Knowledge
segments.gist: There is gold and a multitude of rubies, but the lips of knowledge are a precious jewel; take his garment that is surety for a stranger.

segments.title: Whoso Curseth His Father
segments.gist: Whoso curseth his father or his mother, his lamp shall be put out in obscure darkness; an inheritance may be gotten hastily at the beginning, but the end thereof shall not be blessed.

segments.title: Man's Goings Are of the Lord
segments.gist: Man's goings are of the Lord; how can a man then understand his own way? It is a snare to devour that which is holy, and after vows to make inquiry.

21.summary: Proverbs 21 is a collection of wisdom sayings contrasting the righteous and the wicked, covering themes such as God's sovereignty over rulers, the importance of justice, the dangers of pride and greed, and the value of wise speech and diligence. It emphasizes that no plan or sacrifice can substitute for doing what is right and just.

segments.title: God Weighs Hearts and Deeds
segments.gist: The Lord directs kings' hearts and weighs motives; doing justice pleases him more than sacrifice, while the guilty are devious.

segments.title: Warnings on Strife, Wealth, and Pleasure
segments.gist: Sayings warn about a quarrelsome wife, the wicked's desire for evil, the foolish who ignore wisdom, and the love of pleasure and wine.

segments.title: Righteousness, Diligence, and Speech
segments.gist: The wise store treasure, the wicked are ensnared by their desires, and the righteous give freely; diligence prospers while haste leads to want.

segments.title: No Wisdom Against the Lord
segments.gist: No wisdom, understanding, or counsel can prevail against the Lord; the horse is prepared for battle, but victory comes from him.

22.summary: Proverbs 22 is a collection of wise sayings, mostly contrasting the righteous and the wicked in matters of reputation, wealth, speech, and justice. It includes a series of thirty sayings of the wise (verses 17–29) that give practical instruction on treating the poor, avoiding anger, and honest dealings.

segments.title: Solomon's proverbs on wisdom and wealth
segments.gist: A collection of Solomon's proverbs contrasting the wise and foolish, the rich and poor, and the righteous and wicked in daily life.

segments.title: Introduction to the sayings of the wise
segments.gist: An exhortation to listen to the words of the wise and trust in the Lord, so that truth may be established.

segments.title: Thirty sayings of the wise
segments.gist: A series of practical instructions on justice, speech, friendship, and honest labor, including warnings against oppressing the poor and moving ancient landmarks.

23.summary: Proverbs 23 is a collection of sayings advising restraint and discernment: warnings against greed at a ruler's table, pursuit of wealth, the stingy host, and the seductress; exhortations to discipline children, honor parents, and acquire wisdom; and a closing warning against wine and strong drink.

segments.title: Warning at a Ruler's Table
segments.gist: When dining with a ruler, observe what is before you and restrain your appetite, for his delicacies are deceptive.

segments.title: Do Not Labor for Riches
segments.gist: Do not wear yourself out to get rich; wealth sprouts wings and flies away like an eagle.

segments.title: Bread of a Stingy Host
segments.gist: Do not eat the bread of a stingy man or desire his delicacies, for he is not what he seems and you will lose what you ate.

segments.title: Do Not Speak to a Fool
segments.gist: Do not speak in the hearing of a fool, who will despise your wise words; do not move ancient landmarks or encroach on orphans, for their redeemer is strong.

segments.title: Apply Your Heart to Instruction
segments.gist: Apply your heart to instruction and your ears to knowledge; do not withhold discipline from a child, for wise children bring joy to their parents.

segments.title: Do Not Envy Sinners
segments.gist: Do not envy sinners but fear the Lord, for there is a future hope; do not be among drunkards or gluttons, who come to poverty.

segments.title: Listen to Your Father
segments.gist: Listen to your father and do not despise your mother; buy truth and wisdom, and let your parents rejoice in a wise child.

segments.title: Beware the Seductress
segments.gist: Give me your heart and observe my ways, for a harlot is a deep pit and an adulteress lies in wait to increase the unfaithful.

segments.title: The Woes of Wine
segments.gist: Wine brings woe, sorrow, and strife; it bites like a serpent and leads to strange visions and folly, so do not look at it when it sparkles.

24.summary: Proverbs 24 continues the sayings of the wise, warning against envy of evil men and urging reliance on God's wisdom. It describes the ruin brought by wickedness, the value of wisdom in times of trouble, and the importance of honest labor and just dealings. The chapter ends with a series of observations about the sluggard's field and the dangers of partiality and revenge.

segments.title: Do not envy evil men
segments.gist: Warns against envying evil men or desiring their company, for their hearts devise destruction and their lips speak mischief.

segments.title: Wisdom builds and gives strength
segments.gist: A wise man is strong and increases strength through knowledge and counsel, but the foolish and the scorner are an abomination.

segments.title: Help in the day of trouble
segments.gist: If you faint in adversity, your strength is small; do not ignore the oppressed, for God knows and will repay.

segments.title: Wisdom is sweet; avoid the wicked
segments.gist: Wisdom is sweet to the soul and brings reward; do not lie in wait against the righteous, for the wicked have no future.

segments.title: Fear God and the king
segments.gist: My son, fear the LORD and the king, and do not associate with those who change, for calamity comes suddenly.

segments.title: More sayings of the wise
segments.gist: Further wise sayings: show no partiality, answer wisely, do not avenge, and learn from the sluggard's neglected field.

25.summary: Proverbs 25 is a collection of Solomon's proverbs copied by Hezekiah's men, offering wisdom on kings and courts, patience and self-control, wise speech, and dealing with enemies. It moves from observations about rulers and quarrels to sayings about good news, faithful messengers, and self-restraint.

segments.title: Kings and Court Conduct
segments.gist: Sayings about searching out matters, the king's honor, and behaving wisely before rulers.

segments.title: Avoid Hasty Quarrels
segments.gist: Warnings not to rush into dispute or reveal another's secret, lest you be shamed.

segments.title: Wise and Timely Speech
segments.gist: Comparisons of apt words to gold apples and cool snow, and warnings about false boasts and patient persuasion.

segments.title: Moderation and Consideration
segments.gist: Sayings on eating honey moderately, sparing visits to neighbors, and not exploiting the unfortunate.

segments.title: Dealing with Enemies and Strife
segments.gist: Advice to feed a hungry enemy, warnings about backbiting and a contentious woman, and the value of a good report.

segments.title: Good News and Self-Control
segments.gist: Comparisons of good news to cold water, warnings about yielding to the wicked, and the danger of uncontrolled temper.

26.summary: Proverbs 26 is a collection of sayings contrasting the fool and the sluggard, warning against meddling and deceit, and describing the damage done by a lying tongue, gossip, and hatred. It uses vivid images—a dog returning to its vomit, a madman throwing firebrands—to portray folly and its consequences.

segments.title: Sayings about fools
segments.gist: Honor is unfit for a fool; do not answer or trust a fool; a fool repeats his folly; the lazy man's excuses; a fool is wise in his own eyes.

segments.title: The sluggard's excuses
segments.gist: The slothful man makes absurd excuses to stay in bed and is wiser in his own conceit than seven reasonable men.

segments.title: Meddling and gossip
segments.gist: Interfering in others' quarrels is like grabbing a dog's ears; a deceiver's words are like fire; gossip wounds deeply.

segments.title: Deceit and hatred
segments.gist: Fervent lips with a wicked heart are like earthenware covered with silver dross; hatred is covered by deceit and will be exposed in the congregation; a lying tongue hates those it wounds.

27.summary: Proverbs 27 is a collection of wise sayings on friendship, reputation, and self-control. It warns against boasting, jealousy, and flattery, and praises faithful counsel and honest rebuke. The chapter also touches on diligence, the care of one's possessions, and the hidden depths of the heart.

segments.title: Boasting and Jealousy
segments.gist: Do not boast about tomorrow, and let another praise you rather than your own mouth; jealousy is cruel.

segments.title: Wounds of a Friend
segments.gist: A fool's wrath is heavy, but open rebuke from a friend is better than hidden love or flattery.

segments.title: Value of Counsel
segments.gist: The full soul loathes honey, but the hungry soul finds sweetness; do not forsake your own friend or your father's friend.

segments.title: Prudence and Blessing
segments.gist: Be wise to make your parents glad, avoid the snare of the wicked, and do not bless a neighbor loudly early in the morning.

segments.title: Contentious Woman
segments.gist: A continual dropping on a rainy day and a contentious woman are alike; restraining her is like grasping the wind.

segments.title: Iron Sharpens Iron
segments.gist: Friends sharpen each other, and one who tends a fig tree eats its fruit; the heart of man reflects the man.

segments.title: Care for Flocks
segments.gist: Be diligent to know the state of your flocks, for riches do not last; the hay and grass provide for the goats and sheep.

28.summary: Proverbs 28 is a collection of wisdom sayings contrasting the righteous and the wicked, emphasizing the blessings of integrity, the dangers of greed and oppression, and the importance of confessing sin and trusting in the Lord.

segments.title: Contrasts of Righteous and Wicked
segments.gist: The wicked flee when none pursue, but the righteous are bold; a poor man who oppresses the poor is like a sweeping rain; those who forsake the law praise the wicked, but those who keep the law strive with them; evil men do not understand justice, but those who seek the Lord understand all.

segments.title: Wisdom and Integrity Over Wealth
segments.gist: Better is the poor who walks in integrity than the rich who is perverse; he who keeps the law is a wise son, but a companion of gluttons shames his father; wealth gained by usury and unjust gain will be taken away; he who turns away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer is an abomination; the rich man is wise in his own eyes, but the poor who has understanding sees through him.

segments.title: Blessings of Righteousness, Fall of Wicked
segments.gist: When the righteous triumph, there is great glory, but when the wicked rise, people hide; he who conceals his sins does not prosper, but whoever confesses and forsakes them finds mercy; blessed is the one who fears the Lord always, but the hard-hearted falls into calamity; a wicked ruler over a poor people is like a roaring lion; a prince who lacks understanding is a great oppressor, but one who hates unjust gain will prolong his days; a man burdened with bloodshed will flee to the pit; whoever walks uprightly will be saved, but the perverse will fall suddenly.

segments.title: Diligence, Faithfulness, and Greed
segments.gist: He who tills his land will have plenty of bread, but he who follows worthless pursuits will have poverty; a faithful man will abound with blessings, but he who hastens to be rich will not go unpunished; showing partiality is not good, yet for a piece of bread a man will do wrong; a man with an evil eye hastens after wealth and does not know that poverty will come upon him.

segments.title: Rebuke, Trust, and Final Contrasts
segments.gist: He who rebukes a man will afterward find more favor than he who flatters with the tongue; whoever robs his father or mother and says, 'It is no transgression,' is a companion of a destroyer; he who is greedy for gain troubles his own house, but he who hates bribes will live; the one who trusts in his own heart is a fool, but whoever walks wisely will be delivered; he who gives to the poor will not lack, but he who hides his eyes will have many curses; when the wicked rise, people hide, but when they perish, the righteous increase.

29.summary: Proverbs 29 is a collection of wise sayings contrasting the righteous and the wicked, covering themes such as leadership, justice, discipline, pride, anger, and the fear of man. It emphasizes that the fear of the Lord brings stability and that a ruler who listens to lies will be ruined.

segments.title: Warnings and Wisdom for Rulers
segments.gist: Contrasts the fate of the stiff-necked and the righteous, and describes the characteristics of a just ruler versus a wicked one.

segments.title: Folly, Pride, and Justice
segments.gist: Speaks of scoffers, wise men, fools, the proud, and the importance of justice for the poor and oppressed.

segments.title: Discipline, Prophecy, and Servants
segments.gist: Addresses the need for discipline, the danger of uncontrolled anger, the role of prophets, and the proper treatment of servants.

segments.title: Anger, Pride, and the Fear of Man
segments.gist: Warns about anger, pride, and the fear of man, and contrasts the righteous and the wicked in their dealings with others and with God.

30.summary: Proverbs 30 contains the words of Agur, who confesses his lack of wisdom and asks for neither poverty nor riches, then delivers a series of numerical sayings about insatiable things, a generation that curses its parents, and small but wise creatures, ending with warnings against pride and stirring up strife.

segments.title: Agur's Confession and Request
segments.gist: Agur admits he lacks wisdom, declares God's word pure, and asks for neither poverty nor riches but daily bread.

segments.title: Two Requests Before Death
segments.gist: Agur asks to be kept from vanity and lies and to have neither poverty nor riches lest he deny God or steal.

segments.title: Slander and a Wicked Generation
segments.gist: Warnings against slandering a servant and a description of a generation that curses parents and is haughty and oppressive.

segments.title: Four Insatiable Things
segments.gist: The leech's two daughters and four things that never say 'It is enough': the grave, the barren womb, earth for water, and fire.

segments.title: Four Wonderful and Adulterous Ways
segments.gist: Four things too wonderful to know—an eagle, a serpent, a ship, and a man with a maid—and the adulterous woman who wipes her mouth.

segments.title: Four Things That Trouble the Earth
segments.gist: Four unbearable things: a servant when he reigns, a fool filled with food, an odious woman married, and a handmaid who displaces her mistress.

segments.title: Four Wise but Small Creatures
segments.gist: Ants, conies, locusts, and spiders are small yet exceedingly wise in their ways.

segments.title: Four Stately Walkers
segments.gist: Four things stately in step: a lion, a greyhound, a he-goat, and a king against whom none can rise.

segments.title: Warning Against Pride and Strife
segments.gist: If you have exalted yourself or thought evil, put your hand on your mouth; churning milk brings butter and stirring wrath brings strife.

31.summary: King Lemuel recounts his mother's instruction: warnings against wine and lust for kings, a call to defend the poor, and praise for a virtuous woman whose industry, charity, and fear of the Lord make her worthy of praise.

segments.title: Lemuel's mother's warning
segments.gist: Lemuel's mother advises him to avoid women and wine, which pervert kings, and to judge righteously.

segments.title: The virtuous woman's worth
segments.gist: The virtuous woman is described as far more precious than rubies, trusted by her husband and doing him good.

segments.title: Her industry and provision
segments.gist: She seeks wool and flax, works willingly, brings food from afar, buys a field, plants a vineyard, and makes fine linen.

segments.title: Her charity and wisdom
segments.gist: She cares for the poor, clothes her household in scarlet and silk, speaks with wisdom, and looks well to her household's ways.

segments.title: Praise for the virtuous woman
segments.gist: Her children and husband praise her, and she is honored for fearing the Lord above fleeting beauty.

1.summary: The Preacher opens by declaring all things vanity and cycles endlessly in nature, then laments that human labor gains nothing lasting and that there is no remembrance of past generations.

segments.title: The Preacher's Vanity Declaration
segments.gist: The words of the Preacher, who declares all is vanity and asks what profit labor brings under the sun.

segments.title: Generations and Natural Cycles
segments.gist: Generations pass, the earth remains, and the sun, wind, and rivers move in endless circuits.

segments.title: Weariness and No Remembrance
segments.gist: All things are full of weariness; the eye and ear are unsatisfied, and past generations are forgotten.

segments.title: The Preacher's Search for Wisdom
segments.gist: The Preacher, king over Israel, set his heart to seek wisdom and saw the crooked cannot be made straight.

segments.title: Wisdom as Vexation of Spirit
segments.gist: The Preacher concludes that much wisdom brings grief and increased knowledge brings sorrow.

2.summary: The Preacher tests pleasure, wine, great building projects, wealth, and music, yet finds all of it vanity and no lasting profit. He reflects that the wise and the fool share the same fate, death, and that all a man's labor is ultimately left to another. He concludes that there is nothing better than to eat, drink, and enjoy one's work as a gift from God, since joy and wisdom come from Him alone.

segments.title: Testing pleasure and great works
segments.gist: The Preacher tries laughter, wine, building, gardens, wealth, and music, but finds all is vanity and no profit.

segments.title: Wisdom and folly compared
segments.gist: He turns to consider wisdom and madness, yet sees that the wise and the fool both die and are forgotten.

segments.title: Labor left to another
segments.gist: He hates his labor because he must leave its fruits to a successor, and all his days are sorrow and vexation.

segments.title: Enjoyment as God's gift
segments.gist: He concludes that eating, drinking, and enjoying one's work is from God's hand, who gives wisdom and joy to the good.

3.summary: The Preacher declares that every event in human life has its appointed time, from birth to death and from planting to uprooting. He observes that God has set eternity in the human heart yet people cannot fully grasp His work, and he concludes that there is nothing better than to rejoice and do good. The chapter closes by noting that God's judgments endure and that humans, like beasts, share the same breath and return to dust.

segments.title: A Time for Everything
segments.gist: A poetic list of paired opposites shows that every human activity has its divinely appointed season.

segments.title: God's Eternal Purpose
segments.gist: The Preacher reflects on the profit of labor, God's gift of eternity in the heart, and the call to rejoice and do good.

segments.title: Judgment and Mortality
segments.gist: The Preacher observes injustice, affirms God's judgment, and compares the fate of humans and beasts, concluding that man should enjoy his labor.

4.summary: The Preacher observes oppression and the tears of the oppressed with no comforter, then praises the dead over the living and the unborn over both. He reflects on envy-driven labor, the value of companionship over solitary toil, and the fleeting nature of popular acclaim.

segments.title: Oppression and the Unborn
segments.gist: The Preacher sees the tears of the oppressed with no comforter and concludes the dead and the unborn are better off than the living.

segments.title: Envy and Foolish Toil
segments.gist: He observes that labor springs from envy, calls it vanity, and contrasts the fool's folded hands with a quiet handful.

segments.title: Two Are Better Than One
segments.gist: He praises companionship: two have better reward, can help each other up, keep warm, and defend against an attacker.

segments.title: The Poor Wise Child and the King
segments.gist: A poor wise child succeeds an old foolish king, yet the later generation does not rejoice in him either, showing all is vanity.

5.summary: Ecclesiastes 5 warns against rash speech in God's house and the vanity of wealth, then praises the quiet enjoyment of one's labor as God's gift. It closes by affirming that the ability to enjoy life is from God's hand.

segments.title: Reverence in God's House
segments.gist: Be careful in worship, keep vows, and fear God rather than multiply words.

segments.title: Oppression and Profit
segments.gist: Do not marvel at oppression, for higher officials watch over others and the king profits from the land.

segments.title: Vanity of Wealth
segments.gist: The love of money is never satisfied, and riches bring anxiety, insomnia, and loss.

segments.title: Enjoyment as God's Gift
segments.gist: It is good to eat, drink, and enjoy one's labor, for such enjoyment comes from God's hand.

6.summary: Ecclesiastes 6 reflects on the vanity of wealth and possessions when they cannot be enjoyed, the insatiability of human desire, and the inability to change one's lot or know what is truly good for a person during their brief life.

segments.title: Wealth Without Enjoyment
segments.gist: The Preacher observes the evil of riches given without the power to enjoy them, and the tragedy of a man who has everything yet lacks satisfaction.

segments.title: Insatiable Desire
segments.gist: All man's labor is for his mouth, yet his appetite is never satisfied; the wise and the fool alike find no lasting gain.

segments.title: Who Knows What Is Good?
segments.gist: What exists has already been named, and man cannot contend with the Almighty; who knows what is good for man in his fleeting life?

7.summary: Ecclesiastes 7 is a collection of wisdom sayings that contrast wisdom with folly, reflecting on death, adversity, and the limits of human understanding. The Preacher commends a sober view of life, warns against extremes, and acknowledges that no one is perfectly righteous.

segments.title: Better Days and Adversity
segments.gist: A good name and the day of death are better than precious ointment and birth; sorrow is better than laughter.

segments.title: Wisdom and Its Limits
segments.gist: Oppression destroys wisdom, and the end of a matter is better than its beginning; wisdom gives life to its possessor.

segments.title: Consider the Work of God
segments.gist: Accept God's providence in prosperity and adversity; avoid extremes, for the one who fears God escapes them all.

segments.title: No One Is Perfectly Righteous
segments.gist: Wisdom strengthens, but no one is perfectly righteous; do not heed all that others say, for you too have cursed others.

segments.title: The Search for Wisdom
segments.gist: The Preacher sought wisdom but found it elusive; he found one upright man among a thousand, but no upright woman, and that God made humans upright but they sought many schemes.

8.summary: The Preacher reflects on wisdom and authority, urging obedience to the king and caution in times of uncertainty. He observes that the wicked often prosper and the righteous suffer, yet concludes that it will ultimately go well for those who fear God, while the wicked will not prolong their days. He also notes that man cannot fully comprehend God's work and that joy and enjoyment are man's portion in life.

segments.title: Wisdom and the King's Command
segments.gist: The Preacher advises keeping the king's command and not being hasty to leave his presence, for the wise heart discerns the proper time and judgment.

segments.title: The Wicked Prosper and the Righteous Suffer
segments.gist: The Preacher observes that the wicked are buried and praised while the righteous are forgotten, and that it sometimes goes well with the wicked and ill with the righteous.

segments.title: Enjoyment and God's Unsearchable Work
segments.gist: The Preacher commends enjoyment of life as man's portion, acknowledges that God's work is beyond human comprehension, and concludes that no one can fully understand it.

9.summary: Ecclesiastes 9 reflects on the common fate of all people, righteous and wicked alike, and the uncertainty of life. It encourages enjoying life's simple pleasures while one can, because the dead have no further reward, and it observes that time and chance affect everyone, with wisdom often going unappreciated.

segments.title: One fate for all
segments.gist: The righteous and wicked share the same fate, and the dead have no more reward or memory.

segments.title: Enjoy life's portion
segments.gist: Live joyfully, eat, drink, and work with all your might, for there is no activity in the grave.

segments.title: Time and chance
segments.gist: The race is not to the swift nor the battle to the strong, for time and chance happen to all.

segments.title: Wisdom ignored
segments.gist: A poor wise man saved a city, yet his wisdom was forgotten; wisdom is better than weapons but easily despised.

10.summary: Ecclesiastes 10 is a collection of wisdom sayings contrasting wisdom and folly. It touches on the dangers of folly in high places, the importance of prudence in daily labor and speech, and the unpredictable nature of life under the sun.

segments.title: Folly and Wisdom in Rulers
segments.gist: A little folly spoils reputation; wisdom and folly are contrasted in the context of rulers and authority.

segments.title: Folly Exalted, Rich Brought Low
segments.gist: An evil observed: folly is set in high places while the rich sit in low places, with servants on horses and princes walking.

segments.title: Dangers of Labor and Skill
segments.gist: Various labors carry risks; wisdom and skill are needed to avoid harm and to succeed in work.

segments.title: Words of the Wise and Foolish
segments.gist: The words of a wise man are gracious, but a fool's talk is foolish and self-destructive, multiplying words without knowledge.

segments.title: Woes to the Land and the Value of Diligence
segments.gist: Woe to a land with a childish king and feasting princes; blessing comes with diligent leaders and proper order, and even in thought one should not curse the rich.

11.summary: Ecclesiastes 11 urges bold action despite uncertainty, advising charity, diligence, and joy in youth while remembering that God will judge all deeds and that youth is fleeting.

segments.title: Cast Bread, Work Diligently
segments.gist: Encourages giving freely and working diligently despite not knowing outcomes, for God governs all.

segments.title: Rejoice in Life, Remember Darkness
segments.gist: Exhorts enjoying life's light while remembering that dark days will come.

segments.title: Youth: Rejoice but Remember Judgment
segments.gist: Tells young people to enjoy youth but remember God will judge, so remove sorrow and evil.

12.summary: Ecclesiastes 12 closes the book with a poetic call to remember the Creator in youth, before old age brings physical decline and death, using images of failing strength and a broken golden bowl. It then describes the Preacher's continued teaching of wisdom and ends with the summary that the whole duty of man is to fear God and keep his commandments, for God will bring every work into judgment.

segments.title: Remember Creator in Youth
segments.gist: The Preacher urges remembering God before old age brings failing eyes, limbs, and teeth, using images of declining strength and mourning.

segments.title: Preacher's Wisdom and Warnings
segments.gist: The Preacher, being wise, taught the people knowledge and set forth many proverbs; he warns that much study is a weariness.

segments.title: Fear God and Keep Commandments
segments.gist: The conclusion: fear God and keep his commandments is the whole duty of man, for God will judge every work.

1.summary: The opening chapter of the Song of Solomon presents a dialogue of longing between a Shulamite woman and her beloved, interspersed with the daughters of Jerusalem. She expresses her desire for his kisses and her insecurity about her dark skin, then seeks him and praises his love, while he responds with admiration and invites her to follow.

segments.title: The woman's opening longing
segments.gist: The Shulamite expresses her desire for the king's kisses and asks to be drawn after him, praising his love.

segments.title: She addresses the daughters of Jerusalem
segments.gist: She describes her dark but comely appearance, explains her brothers' anger, and asks where her beloved feeds his flock.

segments.title: The beloved praises her beauty
segments.gist: The man compares her to a company of horses and praises her cheeks and neck adorned with ornaments.

segments.title: The woman speaks of her beloved
segments.gist: She describes the king at his table and her beloved as a bundle of myrrh and a cluster of camphire.

segments.title: Mutual admiration
segments.gist: The man calls her fair with doves' eyes, and she responds that he is fair, describing their green bed and cedar beams.

2.summary: The Shulammite woman speaks of her beloved as a lily among thorns and describes his embrace at a banquet, while he calls her his dove and invites her to arise and come away as the winter passes. She urges the daughters of Jerusalem not to stir up love until it pleases, then recalls a night when she sought her beloved and found him, holding him and bringing him to her mother's house.

segments.title: The Rose of Sharon
segments.gist: The woman describes herself as the rose of Sharon and lily of the valleys, and her beloved as a lily among thorns.

segments.title: Banquet and Apple Tree
segments.gist: She compares her beloved to an apple tree among trees and describes sitting under his shadow and being brought to the banqueting house.

segments.title: Charge to the Daughters
segments.gist: She asks to be sustained with flagons and apples, describes his embrace, and charges the daughters of Jerusalem not to stir up love until it pleases.

segments.title: The Beloved Approaches
segments.gist: She hears her beloved's voice and sees him coming leaping over mountains and hills, likened to a roe or young hart.

segments.title: Invitation to Come Away
segments.gist: Her beloved speaks, inviting her to arise and come away because winter is past and flowers appear, calling her his dove in the rock's clefts.

segments.title: Foxes and Mutual Possession
segments.gist: They ask to catch the little foxes that spoil the vines, declare mutual belonging, and she asks him to turn until the day breaks.

3.summary: The chapter opens with the Shulammite woman searching for her beloved through the city at night, asking the watchmen and then finding him and bringing him to her mother's house. It then shifts to a description of Solomon's wedding procession, with his litter and armed guard coming up from the wilderness, culminating in the call to behold the king on his wedding day.

segments.title: Night Search for the Beloved
segments.gist: The woman searches for her beloved in the city streets at night, asking the watchmen but not finding him.

segments.title: Solomon's Wedding Procession
segments.gist: Solomon's litter, surrounded by armed guards, is described as it comes up from the wilderness.

4.summary: The bridegroom praises his beloved's beauty in a series of comparisons, calling her his sister and spouse and inviting her to come with him from Lebanon. He describes her as a garden enclosed and a fountain sealed, and she responds with an invitation for him to enter his garden and eat its fruits.

segments.title: Praise of the Beloved's Beauty
segments.gist: The groom compares his beloved's eyes, hair, teeth, lips, and neck to natural and architectural wonders, declaring her altogether beautiful.

segments.title: Invitation and Garden Imagery
segments.gist: He calls her his sister and spouse, invites her from Lebanon, and describes her as a garden with precious fruits and a well of living waters.

5.summary: The chapter continues the Shulammite's account: she describes her beloved's visit at night, her delay in opening the door, and her search for him through the city, where the watchmen beat her. She then praises his physical beauty in detail to the daughters of Jerusalem, answering their question about what makes him special.

segments.title: The Beloved's Visit and Departure
segments.gist: The woman recounts how her beloved knocked at night, but she delayed opening; by the time she did, he had gone, and she searched for him without success.

segments.title: Praise of the Beloved's Appearance
segments.gist: The woman describes her beloved's physical features in detail, from his head to his mouth, declaring him altogether lovely.

6.summary: The daughters of Jerusalem ask where the Shulamite's beloved has gone, and she answers that he has gone down to his garden. She then describes his beauty and majesty in a series of comparisons, and he responds by praising her as unique and lovely, comparing her to an army with banners.

segments.title: Where is your beloved?
segments.gist: The daughters of Jerusalem ask the Shulamite where her beloved has gone, and she replies that he is in his garden feeding among the lilies.

segments.title: The beloved praises her beauty
segments.gist: The beloved describes the Shulamite's beauty using images of Tirzah, Jerusalem, and an army with banners, praising her eyes, hair, and cheeks.

segments.title: Unique among many
segments.gist: He declares that though there are many queens and concubines, she is unique and is praised by the daughters and queens.

segments.title: Going to the garden
segments.gist: The Shulamite invites her beloved to go to the garden to see the vines and pomegranates, and the daughters call her back to behold her dance.

7.summary: The chapter continues a dialogue in which the beloved's beauty is praised from her feet to her head, followed by her invitation to go into the fields and vineyards together, where she promises her love to him.

segments.title: Praise of the Shulamite's Beauty
segments.gist: The speaker describes the woman's beauty from her feet upward, comparing her to jewels, a heap of wheat, a tower, and a palace.

segments.title: Invitation to the Vineyards
segments.gist: The woman declares she belongs to her beloved and invites him to go with her to the fields and vineyards to see if the vines have budded.

8.summary: The chapter concludes the Song of Solomon with the woman's longing for her beloved and a dialogue with the daughters of Jerusalem. It reflects on the nature of love as strong as death, ending with a call for the beloved to hasten like a gazelle upon the mountains.

segments.title: Woman's longing and charge
segments.gist: The woman expresses her desire for her beloved and charges the daughters of Jerusalem not to stir up love until it pleases.

segments.title: Who is this coming up?
segments.gist: A question about the woman coming from the wilderness leads to a declaration of love's strength and jealousy.

segments.title: Brothers and the wall
segments.gist: The brothers ask what they shall do for their sister, and she responds that she is a wall and has found peace.

segments.title: Solomon's vineyard
segments.gist: Solomon's vineyard is mentioned, and the woman says her own vineyard is before her.

segments.title: Call to hasten
segments.gist: The woman invites her beloved to be like a gazelle and come quickly over the mountains.

1.summary: Isaiah opens with a prophetic indictment of Judah and Jerusalem for rebellion and empty ritual, calling them to repentance and promising cleansing, but warning that continued disobedience will bring sword and fire. The chapter closes with a lament over Zion's corruption and a promise of restoration through judgment.

segments.title: The Lord's Indictment of Israel
segments.gist: The Lord calls heaven and earth to witness Israel's rebellion, describing the nation as a sinful people who have forsaken Him and are stricken from head to foot.

segments.title: Empty Rituals and Call to Repentance
segments.gist: The Lord rejects sacrifices and festivals without obedience, urging the people to wash, cease evil, learn good, and seek justice; He offers cleansing and forgiveness if they obey.

segments.title: Zion's Corruption and Restoration
segments.gist: Jerusalem is lamented as a faithful city turned harlot; the Lord will purge away dross, restore righteous judges, redeem Zion, and destroy the wicked.

2.summary: Isaiah describes the future exaltation of the Lord's house on Mount Zion, when nations will seek God's ways and peace will prevail. He then condemns Judah for adopting foreign idolatry and calls for humility before the Lord's coming day of judgment against all that is proud and lofty.

segments.title: Mountain of the Lord's House
segments.gist: In the last days, the Lord's house will be established on a high mountain, and many nations will flow to it to learn God's ways and walk in His paths.

segments.title: Call to Walk in the Light
segments.gist: Jacob is called to walk in the light of the Lord, but the people are filled with eastern ways, soothsayers, and idols, and are brought low.

segments.title: Day of the Lord Against the Proud
segments.gist: The proud and lofty will be brought low on the day of the Lord, which is against all that is exalted, so that the Lord alone may be exalted.

segments.title: Idols Abolished; Cease from Man
segments.gist: The idols will completely pass away, and people will hide in caves from the terror of the Lord, so they are told to cease from trusting in man.

3.summary: Isaiah 3 pronounces judgment on Judah and Jerusalem: the LORD will remove their leaders and provisions, leaving them to be ruled by inexperienced youths and oppressors. The chapter then indicts the leaders for grinding the poor and the women for their haughty luxury, contrasting their finery with coming shame and disaster.

segments.title: Judgment on Judah's Leaders
segments.gist: The LORD will take away Judah's supply of bread and water and remove its mighty men, judges, prophets, and elders, leaving youths and base men to rule.

segments.title: Indictment of Oppressive Rulers
segments.gist: Jerusalem and Judah are ruined because their words and deeds provoke the LORD; the leaders are charged with grinding the poor and spoiling the vineyard.

segments.title: Judgment on Haughty Women
segments.gist: The LORD will strike the daughters of Zion with a scab and take away their finery, replacing their ornaments and luxuries with baldness, sackcloth, and branding.

segments.title: Desolation of Zion
segments.gist: The men of Judah will fall by the sword, and Zion's gates will lament and mourn as the city sits desolate.

4.summary: Isaiah 4 continues the oracle of judgment and restoration for Zion. It describes the humiliation of the women of Jerusalem and the cleansing of filth from the city by a spirit of judgment and burning, leading to a holy remnant called Zion's inhabitants, who will be protected by a cloud and fire and dwell in a tabernacle of glory.

segments.title: Cleansing of Zion
segments.gist: The branch of the Lord will be beautiful for survivors, and the Lord will wash away Jerusalem's filth by a spirit of judgment and burning.

segments.title: Cloud and Fire Protection
segments.gist: The Lord will create a cloud by day and fire by night over Mount Zion, serving as a canopy and shelter from storm and rain.

5.summary: Isaiah 5 presents a parable of a vineyard that yields wild grapes despite the owner's care, pronouncing judgment on Judah. It then lists six woes against social injustices and corruption, and concludes with a series of oracles describing the coming Assyrian invasion as God's instrument of judgment.

segments.title: Parable of the Vineyard
segments.gist: God's beloved plants a vineyard with great care, but it yields wild grapes, prompting a judgment on what more could have been done.

segments.title: Woes on Injustice and Excess
segments.gist: Isaiah pronounces woes on those who accumulate houses and fields, drink wine, and ignore God's work, leading to exile and humiliation.

segments.title: Woes on Mockery and Corruption
segments.gist: Woes are declared on those who drag sin with cords of vanity, call evil good, and justify the wicked for bribes.

segments.title: Judgment Like Fire
segments.gist: Because they rejected God's law, the people will be consumed like stubble, and God's anger is not turned away.

segments.title: Assyrian Invasion
segments.gist: God summons a distant nation whose armies are swift and mighty, roaring like lions and bringing darkness and distress.

6.summary: In the year King Uzziah died, Isaiah sees the Lord on a high throne, attended by seraphim, and is overwhelmed by his own and his people's uncleanness. A seraph touches his lips with a live coal, his sin is purged, and he volunteers to be sent. God then tells him to preach to a people who will not understand or turn, and that the land will be laid waste until a holy seed remains.

segments.title: Isaiah's Vision of the Lord
segments.gist: Isaiah sees the Lord on a high throne, with seraphim crying 'Holy, holy, holy' and the house filled with smoke.

segments.title: Isaiah's Confession and Cleansing
segments.gist: Isaiah confesses his unclean lips and those of his people; a seraph touches his mouth with a live coal, declaring his sin purged.

segments.title: The Hardening Message
segments.gist: God commands Isaiah to make the people's hearts dull, ears heavy, and eyes shut, lest they turn and be healed.

segments.title: Desolation and Holy Seed
segments.gist: Isaiah asks how long; God answers until cities are wasted and people exiled, but a tenth will remain as a holy seed.

7.summary: During the Syro-Ephraimite crisis, Isaiah is sent to reassure King Ahaz that the alliance of Rezin and Pekah will not succeed, but Ahaz refuses to ask for a sign. Isaiah then declares that the Lord himself will give a sign: a virgin will conceive and bear a son named Immanuel, and before the child knows right from wrong, the threatening kings will be gone; yet Assyria will later bring devastation upon Judah.

segments.title: Isaiah reassures Ahaz
segments.gist: Isaiah meets Ahaz at the conduit and tells him that the allied kings will not prevail, urging him to trust and ask for a sign.

segments.title: The Immanuel sign
segments.gist: Ahaz refuses to ask, so Isaiah declares the Lord's sign: a virgin will bear a son called Immanuel, and before he knows good and evil the land will be forsaken.

segments.title: Assyria's coming devastation
segments.gist: The Lord will bring Assyria upon Judah, and the land will become desolate, with briers and thorns replacing cultivated fields.

8.summary: Isaiah is told to write a name on a tablet as a sign, and he and his wife bear a son named Maher-shalal-hash-baz, foretelling Assyria's swift plunder of Damascus and Samaria. The LORD warns Judah that Assyria will sweep through the land like a flood, and the people are told to fear God rather than conspiracies, with the prophet and his children as signs. The chapter closes with a warning against seeking mediums, describing a people left in darkness and distress.

segments.title: The Sign of Maher-shalal-hash-baz
segments.gist: The LORD instructs Isaiah to write a name on a tablet and call reliable witnesses, foretelling the plunder of Damascus and Samaria by Assyria before the child can speak.

segments.title: Assyria as a Flood
segments.gist: The LORD warns that because the people rejected the gentle waters of Shiloah, the king of Assyria will come like a flood, overflowing and reaching even to the neck, covering Immanuel's land.

segments.title: Nations Will Be Broken
segments.gist: The prophet calls the nations to assemble and be broken, to gird themselves but be shattered, for God is with us.

segments.title: Fear God, Not Conspiracies
segments.gist: The LORD speaks to Isaiah with a strong hand, warning him not to follow the people's fear or call things conspiracies, but to fear the LORD of hosts, who will be a sanctuary and a stone of stumbling.

segments.title: Seal the Law Among Disciples
segments.gist: Isaiah binds the testimony and seals the law among his disciples, waiting for the LORD who hides His face, and presents himself and his children as signs in Israel.

segments.title: Darkness for Those Who Seek Mediums
segments.gist: The people are told to seek God rather than mediums and wizards; those who lack God's word will wander in darkness, distress, and hunger, cursing their king and God.

9.summary: Isaiah 9 moves from the promise of light to the people walking in darkness, the birth of a child who will reign on David's throne, and a prophetic indictment of Israel's pride and injustice. It declares God's judgment on the northern kingdom through Assyria and on the leaders who mislead the people, ending with a refrain of unrelenting anger.

segments.title: Light and the Child Born
segments.gist: The people in darkness see a great light, and a child is born who will rule with justice and peace on David's throne forever.

segments.title: Judgment on Samaria's Pride
segments.gist: The Lord sends a word against Jacob; the people's pride and alliances will not save them from enemy invasion.

segments.title: Leaders and False Prophets Condemned
segments.gist: The Lord will cut off head and tail—elders and false prophets—because they mislead the people and show no mercy.

segments.title: Wickedness Consumes the Land
segments.gist: Wickedness burns like fire, and the people devour one another; God's anger is not turned away.

10.summary: Isaiah pronounces woe on unjust lawmakers and judges who oppress the poor, warning that Assyria is merely God's rod of anger against hypocritical Israel and will itself be judged for its arrogance. God promises a remnant will return and that the burden will be lifted, while the advancing Assyrian army is described as a forest that the Lord will cut down.

segments.title: Woe to Unjust Rulers
segments.gist: God condemns those who decree unjust laws and deprive the needy of justice, asking what they will do in the day of visitation.

segments.title: Assyria as God's Rod
segments.gist: Assyria is called the rod of God's anger, sent against a hypocritical nation, but its king boasts of conquering kingdoms and their gods.

segments.title: Assyria's Pride Judged
segments.gist: After the Lord finishes His work on Zion, He will punish the arrogant king of Assyria, who boasts of his own strength and wisdom, and the light of Israel will consume his thorns.

segments.title: Remnant Will Return
segments.gist: In that day a remnant of Israel will rely on the Lord, and though the people are many, only a remnant will return as decreed.

segments.title: Burden Lifted from Israel
segments.gist: God tells His people not to fear Assyria, for in a little while His indignation will end and the yoke will be destroyed because of the anointing.

segments.title: Assyrian Army Advances
segments.gist: The Assyrian army is pictured marching through towns toward Jerusalem, but the Lord will cut down the forest with an iron axe and the mighty will fall.

11.summary: Isaiah 11 describes the coming of a righteous shoot from Jesse's stump, upon whom the Spirit of the LORD will rest, who will judge with justice and bring peace to creation. It portrays a restored remnant of Israel and Judah gathered from the nations, with harmony among enemies and a highway for the returning exiles.

segments.title: The Righteous Branch from Jesse
segments.gist: A shoot from Jesse's stump will be endowed with the Spirit and will judge the poor with righteousness and strike the earth with his mouth.

segments.title: Peace in the Animal Kingdom
segments.gist: Predator and prey will live together in harmony, and a little child will lead them, for the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD.

segments.title: The Root as a Banner
segments.gist: The root of Jesse will stand as a banner for the peoples, and the Lord will gather the outcasts of Israel and Judah from the four corners of the earth.

segments.title: Ephraim and Judah United
segments.gist: Ephraim's jealousy will cease, and Judah and Ephraim will join forces to subdue their enemies to the east and west.

segments.title: A Highway for the Remnant
segments.gist: The Lord will dry up the Egyptian sea and the Euphrates River to create a highway for the remnant returning from Assyria.

12.summary: Isaiah 12 is a short song of praise and thanksgiving that the people of God will sing in the day of salvation. It declares that God's anger has turned away, that he is the source of salvation, and that his deeds are to be made known among the nations.

segments.title: Praise for God's Comfort
segments.gist: The singer gives thanks to God, acknowledging that though he was angry, his anger is turned away and he comforts his people.

segments.title: Draw Water with Joy
segments.gist: The people are called to draw water from the wells of salvation with joy and to give thanks and call upon God's name.

segments.title: Sing and Shout Aloud
segments.gist: The inhabitants of Zion are urged to sing praises to God and shout aloud, for great is the Holy One of Israel among them.

13.summary: Isaiah 13 is a prophecy against Babylon, declaring that God will muster an army from a distant land to overthrow the city. It describes the terror of the day of the Lord, with cosmic signs and widespread destruction, and concludes with Babylon's fall to the Medes and its permanent desolation.

segments.title: The Lord Musters His Army
segments.gist: God calls his consecrated ones and mighty warriors to gather on the mountains for battle, signaling the day of the Lord is near.

segments.title: Terror of the Day of the Lord
segments.gist: The day of the Lord brings destruction from the Almighty, with fear, pain, and cosmic disturbances as God punishes the world for its evil.

segments.title: Babylon's Inhabitants Flee and Are Slain
segments.gist: The people flee like hunted gazelles, and the invading army shows no mercy, killing even infants and plundering homes.

segments.title: Babylon's Permanent Desolation
segments.gist: Babylon will be overthrown like Sodom and Gomorrah, left uninhabited forever, with wild animals dwelling in its ruins.

14.summary: Isaiah 14 continues the oracle against Babylon, depicting the fall of its king from lofty pride to the grave, and then shifts to a brief prophecy against Assyria and a lament over Philistia.

segments.title: Israel's Restoration Promised
segments.gist: The Lord will have mercy on Jacob, restore them to their land, and strangers will join them.

segments.title: Taunt Against Babylon's King
segments.gist: Israel will taunt the king of Babylon, describing his fall from power and the grave's welcome.

segments.title: Fall of the Day Star
segments.gist: The shining one is cut down for exalting himself above God, brought low to the pit.

segments.title: Mockery of the Fallen King
segments.gist: Onlookers mock the fallen king, noting his ruined city and denied burial among kings.

segments.title: Babylon's Utter Destruction
segments.gist: The Lord declares He will cut off Babylon's name and remnant, making it a possession for bitterns.

segments.title: Assyria Broken, Philistia Warned
segments.gist: The Lord swears to break Assyria and warns Philistia not to rejoice, for a serpent will come.

15.summary: Isaiah 15 is a lament over Moab, announcing its sudden devastation and the widespread mourning of its people. The prophet describes cities like Ar and Kir falling in a night, refugees fleeing to Zoar and Eglaim, and the waters of Dimon running with blood, with further judgment still to come.

segments.title: Moab's Sudden Devastation
segments.gist: Ar and Kir are laid waste in a night, and Moab's people wail in the streets and on their housetops.

segments.title: Refugees Flee to Zoar
segments.gist: Moab's fugitives flee weeping to Zoar and Eglaim, while the waters of Nimrim are desolate and their goods are carried away.

segments.title: Dimon's Waters Turn to Blood
segments.gist: A cry of distress reaches to Eglaim and Beer-elim, and the waters of Dimon are filled with blood, with more judgment to follow.

16.summary: This chapter continues the oracle against Moab, beginning with a call for Moab to send tribute to Zion and offering refuge to outcasts. It then laments the destruction of Moab's cities and harvest, with the prophet weeping for Moab's refugees, and concludes with a declaration that Moab's pride will be brought low and that within three years its glory will be despised.

segments.title: Moab Urged to Seek Zion
segments.gist: Moab is told to send tribute and to shelter Judah's outcasts, with a promise of a throne established in mercy.

segments.title: Lament for Moab's Ruin
segments.gist: The prophet weeps for Moab's devastated fields and cities, and declares that its prayers to idols will fail.

segments.title: Moab's Glory Soon Cut Off
segments.gist: The Lord declares that within three years Moab's glory will be despised and its remnant few.

17.summary: Isaiah 17 is a prophecy against Damascus, declaring that Syria's capital will be destroyed and its cities abandoned. The oracle extends to Ephraim (the northern kingdom of Israel), whose glory will fade and whose harvest will be like gleanings, yet a remnant will turn to the Lord. The chapter closes with a picture of invading nations roaring like the sea, but they will be scattered by God's rebuke.

segments.title: Damascus to be destroyed
segments.gist: The burden of Damascus: the city will become a ruinous heap, and its cities will be forsaken.

segments.title: Ephraim's glory fades
segments.gist: The glory of Jacob will be made thin, and Ephraim will be like a harvest with only gleanings left.

segments.title: Remnant looks to God
segments.gist: In that day people will look to their Maker and not to the altars and images they made.

segments.title: Cities desolate for forgetting God
segments.gist: The strong cities will be desolate because they forgot the God of their salvation and did not remember the Rock of their strength.

segments.title: Nations roar but are scattered
segments.gist: Many nations roar like the sea, but God rebukes them, and they flee like chaff before the wind, leaving desolation behind.

18.summary: Isaiah 18 is a prophecy concerning the land of Ethiopia (Cush), describing a people tall and smooth-skinned who send envoys by sea. The chapter depicts the LORD's quiet watchfulness from His dwelling place, followed by a sudden harvest-like judgment, and concludes with the Ethiopians bringing a present to the LORD at Mount Zion.

segments.title: Ethiopia's Envoys Sent by Sea
segments.gist: Woe to the land of whirring wings beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, which sends ambassadors by sea in papyrus vessels to a tall, smooth-skinned nation.

segments.title: The LORD Watches Quietly
segments.gist: The LORD declares He will be quiet and watch from His dwelling like clear heat and a cloud of dew, then cut down the shoots and leave them to the birds and beasts.

19.summary: Isaiah delivers a prophecy against Egypt: internal strife and a harsh ruler will bring the nation low, the Nile will dry up and the economy collapse, and Egypt's wise men and idols will be confounded. Yet the chapter ends with a vision of Egypt, Assyria, and Israel worshiping the LORD together and being called a blessing in the earth.

segments.title: The LORD rides into Egypt
segments.gist: The LORD comes against Egypt; idols tremble, the Egyptians' hearts melt, and they are stirred to civil strife and a cruel ruler.

segments.title: The Nile dries up
segments.gist: The waters of the Nile fail, the river turns foul, and Egypt's fishing, flax, and weaving industries collapse.

segments.title: Wise men confounded
segments.gist: Egypt's princes and wise men are exposed as foolish; the LORD mixes a spirit of perverseness so that Egypt staggers in all its works.

segments.title: Egypt fears Judah
segments.gist: In that day Egypt will be afraid of Judah because of the LORD's purpose against it.

segments.title: Egypt turns to the LORD
segments.gist: Five cities speak Canaan's language and swear to the LORD; Egypt builds an altar, cries to the LORD, and is healed and restored.

segments.title: Egypt, Assyria, Israel blessed
segments.gist: A highway joins Egypt and Assyria; the LORD blesses them together with Israel as a blessing in the earth.

20.summary: The LORD instructs Isaiah to walk stripped and barefoot as a sign against Egypt and Ethiopia. After three years, Isaiah explains that the king of Assyria will lead away Egyptian and Ethiopian captives naked and barefoot, and the people of Judah will be dismayed, realizing their trust in Egypt was misplaced.

segments.title: Isaiah's sign act
segments.gist: The LORD commands Isaiah to remove sackcloth and sandals and walk stripped and barefoot.

segments.title: Three-year sign against Egypt
segments.gist: Isaiah's stripped and barefoot walk serves as a three-year sign and wonder against Egypt and Ethiopia.

segments.title: Assyria leads captives away
segments.gist: The king of Assyria will lead Egyptian and Ethiopian captives naked and barefoot, and Judah will be dismayed, saying, 'Behold, such is our expectation.'

21.summary: Isaiah delivers three oracles: the fall of Babylon, described as a watchman's report of the night and the collapse of idols; a brief oracle against Edom (Dumah) and Arabia, answering how long the night will last; and a final word that Arabia's glory will fade within a year.

segments.title: The Burden of the Desert of the Sea
segments.gist: Isaiah sees a terrifying vision of Elam and Media attacking Babylon, and the watchman announces the fall of Babylon and its idols.

segments.title: Oracle Concerning Dumah
segments.gist: A voice from Seir asks the watchman how much of the night remains; he answers that morning comes but also night, and invites the questioner to return.

segments.title: Oracle Concerning Arabia
segments.gist: Arabians are told to lodge in the forest and bring water to fugitives; within a year their glory will fail, as the Lord has spoken.

22.summary: Isaiah delivers a prophecy against Jerusalem, called the valley of vision, condemning the people's carnal confidence and refusal to repent despite the threat of invasion. The chapter then turns to Shebna, the royal steward, who is denounced for his pride and replaced by Eliakim, a figure of future security.

segments.title: Prophecy Against the Valley of Vision
segments.gist: Isaiah declares that the valley of vision will be invaded, causing panic and flight, yet the people do not look to God.

segments.title: People's False Security and Refusal to Mourn
segments.gist: The people rely on their own defenses and indulge in feasting instead of mourning, so the iniquity will not be forgiven.

segments.title: Shebna's Pride and Coming Judgment
segments.gist: The Lord rebukes Shebna, the steward, for carving a tomb for himself, and foretells his removal and exile.

segments.title: Eliakim's Promotion and Fall
segments.gist: Eliakim is raised up as a father to Jerusalem, given authority, but even he will eventually be cut down.

23.summary: Isaiah delivers a prophecy against Tyre, declaring that the city's wealth and trade will be destroyed by the Chaldeans. After seventy years of desolation, Tyre will be restored, but its profits will be dedicated to the LORD and will benefit those who dwell before Him.

segments.title: Lament for Tyre's Fall
segments.gist: The ships of Tarshish are called to wail because Tyre, the great merchant city, is laid waste and its traders are struck with silence.

segments.title: Tyre's Pride and Judgment
segments.gist: Tyre is told to flee to Tarshish, and the LORD's purpose is to stain the pride of all glory, bringing down the city's strength.

segments.title: Chaldeans Destroy Tyre
segments.gist: The Chaldeans are described as the instrument of Tyre's destruction, and the ships of Tarshish are again told to howl.

segments.title: Tyre Restored After Seventy Years
segments.gist: After seventy years, Tyre will be restored like a harlot's song, and its merchandise will be holy to the LORD, supporting those who dwell before Him.

24.summary: Isaiah 24 depicts the LORD's devastating judgment on the whole earth, overturning social order and laying waste the land because its inhabitants have broken the everlasting covenant. A remnant lifts up songs of praise amid the ruin, but the prophet foresees terror, pit, and snare until the LORD punishes the host of the high ones and the kings of the earth, reigning in glory on Mount Zion.

segments.title: The LORD Empties the Earth
segments.gist: The LORD is described as emptying, spoiling, and scattering the earth's inhabitants, with no distinction between people and priest, servant and master.

segments.title: Joy Fails and the City Is Broken
segments.gist: The wine and music cease, the city is broken down, and a remnant in the midst of the earth lifts up songs of praise.

segments.title: Songs of Praise from the Remnant
segments.gist: Those who remain lift up their voice and sing for the majesty of the LORD, but the prophet laments his leanness and the treachery of the earth.

segments.title: Terror, Pit, and Snare
segments.gist: Terror, pit, and snare come upon the earth's inhabitants; the earth reels like a drunkard and falls, never to rise again.

segments.title: The LORD Punishes and Reigns in Zion
segments.gist: The LORD punishes the host of the high ones and the kings of the earth, and reigns in glory on Mount Zion before his elders.

25.summary: Isaiah 25 is a song of praise for God's deliverance, celebrating the destruction of a strong city and the refuge He provides for the poor. It culminates in a vision of a universal feast on Mount Zion where God swallows up death and wipes away tears, followed by a declaration of victory over Moab.

segments.title: Praise for God's Deliverance
segments.gist: The prophet praises God for His faithful plans, which have turned a strong city into a ruin and become a refuge for the poor and needy.

segments.title: Feast and Victory over Death
segments.gist: On Mount Zion, God prepares a feast for all peoples and swallows up death forever, wiping away tears and removing His people's reproach.

segments.title: Rejoicing and Moab's Humiliation
segments.gist: The people rejoice in God's salvation, while Moab is trampled down and its fortified walls are brought low.

26.summary: Isaiah 26 is a song of praise and trust in God, celebrating His salvation and righteous judgments. It contrasts the fate of the righteous, who are kept in peace, with the wicked, who are brought low. The chapter concludes with a call for God's people to wait for Him and a promise of resurrection.

segments.title: Song of Trust in God
segments.gist: The righteous nation praises God for salvation and strength, and the lofty city is brought down.

segments.title: The Way of the Just
segments.gist: The prophet describes the righteous path and God's judgments, contrasting the wicked who do not learn righteousness.

segments.title: God's Peace and Increase
segments.gist: The people acknowledge God's peace and increase, and recall how He has subdued their enemies.

segments.title: Prayer in Distress and Promise of Resurrection
segments.gist: In distress the people pray, and God promises that the dead shall live and the earth shall cast out the dead.

segments.title: Call to Hide Until Wrath Passes
segments.gist: God's people are told to hide until His indignation passes and He comes to punish the earth's inhabitants.

27.summary: Isaiah 27 presents a future deliverance in which the LORD punishes Leviathan, protects and nurtures his vineyard Israel, and calls his people to worship him in Jerusalem. It promises the ingathering of exiles, the removal of idols, and the forgiveness of iniquity, ending with a great trumpet blast that brings scattered Israelites home.

segments.title: The LORD keeps his vineyard
segments.gist: The LORD sings of his vineyard, promising to water and guard it, and calls his people to make peace with him.

segments.title: Jacob's iniquity purged
segments.gist: The LORD strikes Jacob less than his enemies, and through exile and desolation the iniquity of Jacob is purged and idols are removed.

segments.title: Exiles gathered with a trumpet
segments.gist: In that day a great trumpet sounds, and the LORD gathers the scattered children of Israel to worship him in Jerusalem.

28.summary: Isaiah 28 pronounces judgment on Ephraim's drunken leaders and on Jerusalem's scoffing rulers who have made a covenant with death. Through the prophet, the LORD warns that their false refuge will be swept away, that He will lay a tested cornerstone in Zion, and that His strange work of judgment will come. The chapter ends with a parable of the farmer who varies his methods, illustrating God's discerning dealings with His people.

segments.title: Woe to Drunken Ephraim
segments.gist: The crown of pride of Ephraim's drunkards will be trampled, and the LORD will be a crown of glory to the remnant.

segments.title: Judah's Leaders Stumble
segments.gist: Judah's priests and prophets reel with wine and mock the prophet's message, so God will speak to them with stammering lips and they will fall.

segments.title: Covenant with Death Scorned
segments.gist: Jerusalem's rulers boast of a covenant with death, but the LORD says their refuge will be swept away and He will lay a sure foundation in Zion.

segments.title: Parable of the Farmer
segments.gist: The prophet compares God's varied discipline to a farmer who plows, sows, and threshes with different tools, showing the LORD's wonderful counsel.

29.summary: Isaiah pronounces woe on Ariel (Jerusalem) for its empty religious routine, yet promises that God will defend it and that its enemies will vanish like a dream. He then rebukes the people for treating God's word as a sealed book and for hiding their plans from the Lord, and foretells a day when the deaf will hear, the meek will rejoice, and the house of Jacob will sanctify God's name.

segments.title: Woe to Ariel, but God defends
segments.gist: God will distress Ariel for its formal worship, yet He will fight for it and scatter its foes like dust.

segments.title: Spiritual blindness and sealed vision
segments.gist: The people are blinded; prophets and seers are as a sealed book to those who cannot read it.

segments.title: Lip service and hidden plans
segments.gist: The Lord condemns worship by rote and the people's attempt to hide their counsel from Him.

segments.title: Promise of restoration for the meek
segments.gist: Lebanon will become a fruitful field, the deaf will hear, the meek will rejoice, and Jacob will sanctify God's name.

30.summary: Isaiah 30 pronounces woe on Judah for seeking Egypt's help instead of trusting God, yet promises that God will wait to be gracious and will deliver Jerusalem, destroying Assyria with a supernatural display. It also condemns reliance on false prophets and calls for repentance and trust in quietness.

segments.title: Woe to rebellious children
segments.gist: Judah is condemned for forming an alliance with Egypt without God's counsel, and the burden of their treasures will bring shame.

segments.title: Recorded for a rebellious people
segments.gist: The prophecy is to be written for a rebellious people who reject God's word and trust in oppression, leading to sudden collapse.

segments.title: Salvation in quietness rejected
segments.gist: God offered deliverance through quiet trust, but the people refused, so He will wait to be gracious and exalted in judgment.

segments.title: Promise of restoration
segments.gist: God promises to hear the people's cry, give them teachers, and bless their land with rain and abundant harvest in the day of restoration.

segments.title: Judgment on Assyria
segments.gist: The LORD comes in fierce anger to punish Assyria, and His people will rejoice as He defeats the enemy with fire and sword.

31.summary: Isaiah 31 warns Judah against relying on Egypt's horses and chariots rather than trusting the LORD, who will defend Jerusalem and overthrow Assyria. The chapter calls the people to return to God and promises that the Assyrian threat will be ended by divine intervention.

segments.title: Woe to Those Trusting Egypt
segments.gist: Isaiah pronounces woe on those who go down to Egypt for help, trusting horses and chariots rather than the Holy One of Israel.

segments.title: The LORD Will Defend Zion
segments.gist: The LORD compares Himself to a lion and to birds hovering over Jerusalem, promising to defend and deliver the city.

segments.title: Call to Return from Idols
segments.gist: The people are urged to return to the LORD, and a day is coming when they will cast away their idols of silver and gold.

segments.title: Assyria Will Fall by the Sword
segments.gist: Assyria will fall by a sword not of man, and its young men will flee in terror, declares the LORD whose fire is in Zion.

32.summary: Isaiah 32 describes a future righteous king and his just rule, contrasting it with the complacent and careless women of Jerusalem, and promises the outpouring of the Spirit that will transform the land and bring peace and security.

segments.title: The Righteous King and His Reign
segments.gist: A king will reign in righteousness, providing shelter and justice, and the eyes of those who see will not be dim.

segments.title: Warning to Careless Women
segments.gist: The prophet calls complacent women to hear and tremble, for their fields and houses will be forsaken.

segments.title: The Spirit Poured Out
segments.gist: When the Spirit is poured from on high, the wilderness becomes fruitful and righteousness brings peace and quietness forever.

33.summary: Isaiah 33 is a prophetic oracle that begins with a warning to the destroyer and a prayer for God's intervention. It describes the LORD's exaltation and the terror of sinners in Zion, then shifts to a vision of the righteous king and the security of Jerusalem under God's protection, ending with a picture of Zion's peaceful and glorious future.

segments.title: Woe to the Destroyer and Prayer for Help
segments.gist: The prophet pronounces woe on the treacherous destroyer and prays for God's mercy and intervention, acknowledging God's power and the people's need for deliverance.

segments.title: Desolation and God's Exaltation
segments.gist: The land is in mourning, envoys weep, and God declares He will rise up and be exalted, reducing the enemy's plans to stubble and consuming them like fire.

segments.title: Sinners in Zion Afraid
segments.gist: The sinners in Zion are terrified, asking who can dwell with the consuming fire; the answer is the righteous who walk uprightly and despise oppression.

segments.title: The Righteous King and Secure Zion
segments.gist: The prophet describes the king in his beauty and the security of Zion, where God is judge, lawgiver, and king, and no one says, 'I am sick'; the people are forgiven.

34.summary: Isaiah 34 announces the LORD's fierce judgment on all nations, with Edom singled out as the representative target of His wrath. The chapter describes the slaughter, the desolation of the land, and the perpetual ruin that will follow, contrasting the fate of the wicked with the future inheritance of the redeemed.

segments.title: Judgment on All Nations
segments.gist: The LORD summons the nations to hear His anger, promising total destruction of their armies and the dissolution of the heavens.

segments.title: Edom Slaughtered
segments.gist: God's sword descends on Edom, and the people are slain like sacrificial animals, their land soaked with blood.

segments.title: Edom's Land Desolate
segments.gist: Edom's streams become pitch and its dust brimstone; the land lies waste from generation to generation.

segments.title: Wild Creatures Inhabit Edom
segments.gist: The ruined land is parceled out to desert animals and birds, which nest and thrive among the ruins.

segments.title: Certainty of the Prophecy
segments.gist: The book of the LORD assures that none of these creatures will be missing, for His Spirit gathers them and assigns their portions forever.

35.summary: Isaiah 35 is a prophetic poem describing the future restoration of Zion: the desert will blossom, the weak will be strengthened, God will come with vengeance and save his people, the blind and deaf and lame will be healed, and a highway of holiness will bring the redeemed home to Zion with everlasting joy.

segments.title: Desert Blossoms
segments.gist: The wilderness and desert rejoice and blossom abundantly, displaying the glory of Lebanon and Carmel.

segments.title: Strengthen the Weak
segments.gist: The prophet calls for strengthening weak hands and feeble knees, telling the fearful to be strong because God will come with vengeance and save them.

segments.title: Healing and Water
segments.gist: The eyes of the blind, ears of the deaf, and lame will be healed, and waters will break out in the wilderness and streams in the desert.

segments.title: Highway of Holiness
segments.gist: A highway called the Way of Holiness will be for the redeemed, who return to Zion with singing and everlasting joy, while sorrow and sighing flee away.
